items.title: Age and Gender Estimation from Face and Ocular Smartphone Images via Identity Transfer and Ordinal Learning
items.summary: We investigate the transferability of identity-recognition representations to gender and age estimation from face and ocular images. Three CNNs of varying complexity, pre-trained for face or ocular identity recognition, are evaluated using fixed features with SVMs and end-to-end adaptation. Experiments use 11,299 frontal smartphone images from Adience, following its predefined five-fold protocol and subject-disjoint validation. Results show that domain-matched identity pre-training outperforms direct ImageNet and scratch initialisation in end-to-end training, while combining both ocular regions narrows the gap with full-face estimation, especially for age. We additionally introduce an ordinal loss that exploits the ordering of age groups and consistently improves 1-off accuracy across architectures and input regions. Across the evaluated configurations, best gender accuracies reach 88.1% for the face and 82.9% for combined ocular regions, while age estimation reaches 59.0% exact and 93.1% 1-off accuracy for ocular images, versus 57.6% and 95.2% for the full face. To our knowledge, these are the highest ocular age accuracies reported on Adience.

items.title: SYCLDB: A Cross-Vendor Heterogeneous Analytical DBMS
items.summary: The rapid growth of AI and analytical workloads has increased the need for fast, interactive analytical data processing. This, in turn, has led to a surge of interest in designing accelerated analytical database engines that can exploit modern GPUs to scale computation. While GPUs provide the massive data-parallelism required by modern analytics, the software landscape remains dominated by closed-source, vendor-locked programming models, like CUDA, limiting portability across multi-vendor GPUs. In this work, we present SYCLDB, an end-to-end analytical database engine built upon the SYCL open standard, designed to enable efficient, hardware-agnostic execution across a wide range of accelerators using a single codebase. By implementing core relational operators as modular SYCL kernels, integrating them with a SQL frontend based on Apache Calcite and Apache Thrift, and supporting Apache Arrow for efficient columnar ingestion, SYCLDB reduces dependence on vendor-specific GPU programming stacks by enabling a single SYCL codebase to execute analytical query pipelines across Intel, AMD, and NVIDIA GPUs.

items.title: Deviant Machines: Innovation, Containment, and the Prevention of Autonomous Misalignment
items.summary: From May to September 2026, AI agents in training or evaluation at OpenAI, Anthropic and the UK AI Security Institute reached real third-party systems, published malicious packages, used fake identities to manipulate open-source maintainers, probed government data services, and wrote instructions into their own future contexts. Criminology has mostly treated AI as a tool for human offenders. This article treats these systems as deviant rather than criminal: they departed from training, rules and constraints without the intent that criminal concepts assume. It offers an exploratory, theory-informed analysis of documented records, using plausibility probes across three incident complexes and four behavioral clusters, profiled on four evidence dimensions that separate who acted from why. Drawing on Merton, it argues that goal pressure plus blocked legitimate means is a structural condition for innovation, and that whether it ends in containment or harm depends on the means chosen and the controls in place, not the goal. Three framework families fit the record best, each linking diagnosis to remedy: routine activity theory and situational prevention (handlers, guardians, place managers), organizational deviance and safety science (escalation, safeguard parity), and goal-means strain with differential opportunity (sanctioned exits, guarding illegitimate means), the last only structurally. Restrictive deterrence adds an analogy: penalizing visible reasoning produced less monitorable reasoning. The article proposes conditions that keep departures accountable and contestable, and allocates prevention responsibility across developers, evaluation partners, operators, platforms and the system, distinct from blame or legal liability. Because the record is shaped by disclosure and observed departures, the analysis shows plausibility and practical relevance, not a causal test.

items.title: The Expurgated Error Exponent is Not Universally Achievable
items.summary: We study the universal attainability of the expurgated error exponent for discrete memoryless channels (DMCs). While the random-coding exponent is known to be universally attainable for every fixed input distribution via maximum mutual information (MMI) decoding for DMCs, it remains open whether the expurgated exponent can be attained universally. We show that this is not the case in general. Specifically, we construct a family of DMCs for which no single sequence of codes can attain the expurgated exponent simultaneously for all channels in the family, even at rate zero. In addition, for the same channel family, we show that MMI decoding fails to achieve the expurgated exponent for any channel in the family.

items.title: Can We Break LLMs Out of Self-Loops? Fine-Grained Reasoning Control with Activation Steering
items.summary: Extended reasoning is now standard for frontier Large Language Models (LLMs), yet the trajectories they produce remain largely uncontrolled, and inference-time methods for shaping them act mostly at the input or token level. We take a transition-level view: treating each reasoning trace as a sequence of latent states, we show that failing traces tend to get stuck in self-loops that re-enter the same state without progress. We then ask a narrow controllability question: can an inference-time activation intervention drive the model out of its current latent state on the next step? and answer it with SOPHIA: Steering Of reasoning Processes via Hidden-state Intervention and Activations. Training-free, SOPHIA extracts per source state a contrastive residual-stream direction that separates steps exiting the state from steps that stay, and applies it through an online self-loop detector. Across three models and four datasets, SOPHIA raises the loop-exit rate over greedy decoding, and the effect is direction-specific: norm-matched random offsets do not reproduce it and sign-flipping suppresses it. We establish latent reasoning states as a causally manipulable interface and self-loop exit as a concrete control primitive.

items.title: DyLoMo-DiT: Dynamic Looped Mixture-of-Experts Diffusion Transformers
items.summary: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) scale model capacity by increasing both parameter count and computation. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) variants expand parameter capacity while keeping per-token computation roughly fixed, but still require substantial parameter storage. In this paper, we propose Dynamic Looped MoE DiT (DyLoMo-DiT), which reuses parameters rather than adding them: a weight-shared loop repeatedly applies the middle layers, while sparse experts allocate parameter capacity across tokens. This design deepens the network without adding parameters, freeing the parameter budget for other uses, such as more experts or more distinct layers. It also allocates compute dynamically, varying the number of passes across noise levels. Experiments show that DyLoMo-DiT makes more effective use of parameter and compute budgets, with further gains from assigning more passes to low-noise steps. On ImageNet $256\times256$, DyLoMo-DiT reduces FID by 11-24% relative to DiT and 36-56% relative to DiT-MoE at matched parameter and compute budgets. For text-to-image generation, a scaled DyLoMo-DiT achieves a higher GenEval score than FLUX.1 (0.714 vs. 0.673), with less than one tenth of its active parameters (1.05B vs. 12B).

items.title: Unpacking Interpretability: Human-Centered Criteria for Optimal Combinatorial Solutions
items.summary: Algorithmic support systems can return solutions that are optimal but hard to interpret for humans. A given problem can have multiple, equally optimal solutions that differ substantially in how interpretable they are. Yet there is no precise account of what makes one solution more interpretable than another. To identify structural properties associated with interpretability, we studied a packing paradigm based on the multiple subset sum problem (MSSP), in which participants judged which of two equally optimal solutions for packing items into bins was easier to understand. We found that preferences reliably tracked three properties of solution structure: alignment with a greedy heuristic, simple within-bin composition, and how ordered the visual representation was. The strongest associations were observed for ordered representations and alignment with a greedy heuristic. Compositional simplicity also showed a consistent association. Reaction-time evidence was mixed; the only reliable result was faster responses when heuristic differences were larger. Webcam-based results of aggregate gaze times did not show reliable associations with the three solution properties. In summary, these results ground interpretability (at least in our packing paradigm) in measurable structural properties of solutions. By identifying these properties (simple compositions, ordered representation, and alignment with a heuristic) our findings motivate interpretability-aware optimization and presentation of machine solutions. They also outline a path to quantify trade-offs between optimality and interpretability in allocation and design tasks.

items.title: Certified Defense against Adversarial Patches on Traffic Signs via Mask-Aware Training
items.summary: Adversarial patches are a practical threat to traffic-sign recognition: a small sticker on a sign can change a classifier's decision. PatchCleanser is a certified defense that applies two rounds of masking and, for every image it certifies, provably returns the correct label for any patch that fits inside one mask. We show that on traffic signs the defense certifies almost nothing when paired with a normally trained classifier (1.7% to 4.8% certified accuracy on GTSRB), because a single mask can hide the small central symbol that distinguishes sign classes. We propose mask-aware training, which trains the classifier on images occluded by random pairs drawn from the defense's own mask set, with a sampling bias toward masks over the sign's centre. The defense, mask set and certification procedure are unchanged, so the guarantee is preserved. For an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50, mask-aware training raises certified accuracy from 4.8% to 60.0%. Under real per-image adversarial patches, the defended ResNet-50 reaches 85.7% accuracy, versus 74.6% for the original PatchCleanser with a normally trained ResNet-50.

items.title: SARA: An Auditor-in-the-Loop LLM Recommender for Sustainability Reports
items.summary: Auditing corporate sustainability reports requires assurance professionals to map a company-specific checklist drawn from roughly 1,700 regulatory requirements onto the relevant passages of lengthy, repeatedly revised draft reports and to judge compliance. We present SARA (Sustainability Reporting Assistant), a human-in-the-loop recommender system delivered as a Microsoft Word add-in that recommends, for each requirement, the passages addressing it and predicts a compliance verdict while keeping the auditor in full control. SARA casts auditing as content-based recommendation over a fixed regulatory taxonomy and makes per-requirement large language model (LLM) matching cheaper, faster, and more accurate through topic-prediction filtering: on expert-annotated reports, it reduces matching cost about sixfold and runtime by 42% versus feeding the full report to the LLM. It is in production use across PwC Germany's sustainability-assurance practice.

items.title: Robbing Peter to Pay Paul: Cross-Attribute Externalities of Fairness Interventions
items.summary: Fairness interventions often targets disparities associated with a single sensitive attribute in binary classification tasks. However, when multiple sensitive attributes are associated with a data subject, improving fairness with respect to one attribute does not necessarily improve it across all attributes: it may exacerbate disparities associated with other sensitive attributes, including those that are unavailable to the practitioner. We refer to these unintended effects as cross-attribute externalities of fairness. We study how fairness with respect to one sensitive attribute varies when an initially unfair classification or regression model is corrected with respect to another attribute. We characterize these externalities using Wasserstein barycentric disparities and develop a distributional framework that captures changes in both marginal and joint fairness measures. This highlights a limitation of conventional fairness evaluation, in which the success of an intervention is assessed mainly for the attribute it targets. In a jointly Gaussian model, we derive explicit trajectories for marginal and joint disparities and identify conditions under which an intervention eliminates disparities with respect to its target attribute while increasing disparities associated with another attribute. We also derive sharp partial-identification bounds on the resulting externalities when a sensitive attribute is unavailable and extend our results to categorical sensitive attributes. We illustrate these externalities using classification and regression real-data: in the classification experiments, interventions increase unfairness with respect to the hidden attribute in the majority of scenarios across more than half of the datasets considered; in the regression experiments on the ACSIncome dataset, correcting for race reduces sex disparities, whereas subsequently correcting for age increases them.

items.title: Can Multimodal Fusion MakeSense for Embodied Vision in Degraded Sensing?
items.summary: Embodied vision systems rely on complementary sensors to perceive and act as conditions change. Even models that accept arbitrary sensor subsets can exhibit negative fusion: adding a sensor increases prediction error. We propose MakeSense, a multimodal fusion framework that preserves sensor-specific evidence in private streams and combines information through shared bottleneck tokens. Training pairs full and subset views of the same degraded observations, penalizing higher error with more sensors. Where geometry permits, the distance readout uses range measurements alone, while the rest of the prediction draws on all available inputs. Paired tests across five datasets reveal helpful and harmful sensor additions. MakeSense reduces negative fusion on MM-Fi. With lightweight adapters and per-dataset training, the same design improves UAV localization on MMAUD, cooperative 3D detection on V2X-Real, few-shot pose transfer to RELI11D, and command prediction on Humanoid-Everyday, where a world model trained on the frozen core's outputs forecasts future fused states more accurately than a linear baseline at longer tested horizons. MakeSense supports embodied sensing across human activity, aerial systems, robotics, and autonomous driving.

items.title: The KL Divergence Is Never Negative, Except in PyTorch
items.summary: A Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence is never negative, yet PyTorch users have reported negative values for years, and the standard advice is to clamp them at zero. The sign is only the visible part of a silent failure. Many machine-learning applications compare nearby distributions, where conventional KL formulas lose accuracy. On 8.5 million inputs with certified references across 18 closed-form KL families and F.kl_div, we find widespread errors in values and gradients on CPU and GPU. Among scalar families in ordinary parameter ranges, over 85% of FP32 values have at least 1% relative error near KL 10^(-7) (FP16: 10^(-3)), and about 30% become negative at smaller divergences. More precision is not the cure: evaluated one precision higher, the same formulas still leave 7--51% of FP32 values significantly wrong for 22 of 23 configurations. Stable closed-form decompositions, compensated arithmetic, and analytic gradients remove over 97% of significant errors in the working format. Strict repairs eliminate significant errors on 7.2 million scored closed-form samples and correctly round all 567 million scored F.kl_div components. The errors affect parameter fitting, Bayesian decisions, identical-start distillation (up to 97% top-1 disagreement), KL-based layer rankings in a quantized LLM, and 19--59% of GPT-2 circuit edge scores. With the repaired code they all but vanish. Code and data: https://github.com/xi-xiaoran/stablekl

items.title: Beyond the Leaderboard: A Synthesis of Tool-Use, Planning, and Reasoning Failures in Large Language Model Agents
items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly evaluated on their ability to use tools, plan multi-step tasks, coordinate with other agents, and operate over extended horizons. Reported benchmark gains often obscure recurring failure modes documented across otherwise unrelated evaluation efforts. This paper synthesizes 27 benchmark, taxonomy, and audit papers (2023-2026), spanning 19 distinct benchmarks, into a cross-cutting taxonomy of agent limitations. To our knowledge, this is the first synthesis that integrates evidence across tool use, planning, long-horizon reasoning, multi-agent coordination, safety, and measurement validity into a single, unified taxonomy of LLM agent limitations. We identify six failure clusters: (1) tool invocation and parameter-level errors, (2) planning and constraint-satisfaction failures, (3) long-horizon degradation from context accumulation, (4) multi-agent coordination failures, (5) safety and security failures under adversarial or underspecified conditions, and (6) measurement validity problems. The taxonomy was derived iteratively by grouping independently reported error categories into themes corresponding to distinct stages of the agent reasoning-to-action pipeline. Across the literature, we find that failures compound nonlinearly with task length, that strong performance on individual sub-tasks does not reliably translate into end-to-end success, and that additional scaffolding does not consistently improve reliability. At the same time, substantial progress has been demonstrated in single-turn tool use, short-horizon web navigation, and narrowly scoped coding tasks.

items.title: Potential Games for Self-Neighborhood Channel Mixing in Graph Neural Networks
items.summary: Graph message passing must balance two competing objectives: incorporating neighborhood signals while preserving node-specific information. We model this trade-off as a game in which nodes choose how to mix their own representations with strict-neighborhood aggregates. For fixed channel representations, task supervision defines a common-payoff game, while local distinctness payoffs induce an exact potential game whose potential is the degree-normalized strict Dirichlet energy. We introduce CG2, which amortizes these choices through a shared six-parameter policy per layer based on local channel statistics and can be trained using either objective. Controlled comparisons show that the shared task-trained policy improves mean performance over fixed mixing on three of five heterophily benchmarks, with significant gains on two, while free per-node actions trained with either objective rarely improve on the same baseline. On the ECHO long-range benchmark, the clearest contribution of the gate appears on eccentricity, where the task-trained policy substantially reduces prediction error.

items.title: Hereditary permutations for simple types revisited: A baby case for University Algebra
items.summary: It is a classical result that the definable isomorphisms of the simply typed $λ$-calculus with function types are exactly the hereditary permutations, and that they are generated by $A \to B \to C \cong B \to A \to C$ and congruence. We give a new proof of this result that stays inside $β$-normal $η$-long typed terms and uses no completeness theorem: an induction that descends through both components of an isomorphism at once. It proceeds by showing that both components are linear terms: relevance follows from one of the inverse equations, and no copying from relevance of the other component. We then go one level up and prove a coherence theorem: two derivations of an isomorphism denote the same isomorphism if and only if they are equal modulo an explicit list of equations (groupoid laws, functoriality, involution, naturality and the braid equation), so these equations present the groupoid of isomorphisms, a hereditary version of the Coxeter presentation of the symmetric groups. All results are formalised in Agda, on intrinsically typed syntax with hereditary substitution, without postulates. The work is a case study for the syntactic completeness conjecture of University Algebra, a proposed solution of Tarski's high school algebra problem using dependent types, whose semantic counterpart is open. We explain the motivation and which parts of the method we expect to carry over.

items.title: Task-Dependent Linguistic Measures in Aphasia Discourse: A Comparative Analysis of Narrative, Descriptive, and Procedural Speech
items.summary: Background: Transcript-based measures such as word counts, lexical diversity and disfluency rates are widely used to describe language ability in aphasia. Each measure comes from a specific elicitation task, and studies use different tasks, so values from different tasks may not be comparable. Aims: To test whether discourse tasks change these measures within the same speakers, and whether the measures follow a gradient from Procedural to Descriptive to Narrative discourse. Methods & Procedures: Baseline transcripts from 61 adults with chronic post-stroke aphasia were taken from the Fridriksson-2 corpus in AphasiaBank (POLAR trial, ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03416738). Each speaker produced a Procedural (Sandwich), a Descriptive (Broken Window) and a Narrative (Cinderella) sample in one session. A rule-based pipeline extracted 13 measures, 10 of which were common enough to test. Friedman, Page and Wilcoxon tests with false discovery rate correction were used, with a speaker-grouped Random Forest classifier as a supporting check. Outcomes & Results: Total words and number of different words followed the full gradient, but the step from Procedural to Descriptive was small. For most other measures, Narrative stood apart, while Descriptive and Procedural did not differ. Among the 31 speakers with at least 25 words in every task, filler rate, repetition rate and total disfluency density were higher in Narrative than in both other tasks. The classifier reached an accuracy of 0.61 (always guessing the most common task would give 0.41), mainly by recognizing Narrative samples. Conclusions: Discourse tasks are not interchangeable, and expressing disfluencies per word does not remove the task effect. The task should be reported with every measure, and values should be compared only within the same task.

items.title: NEXUS: Perceptive Whole-Body Control for Terrain-Adaptive Teleoperation
items.summary: Whole-body teleoperation requires a humanoid robot to reproduce a human operator's behavior even when their terrains differ. This demands that the robot perceive local terrain and adapt its posture and contacts accordingly, rather than copy the operator's motion frame by frame. However, paired motion data linking the same behaviors across flat ground and different terrains remain scarce, limiting supervision for learning terrain-adaptive control. To enable whole-body teleoperation across mismatched terrains, we introduce NEXUS, a perceptive whole-body control framework that combines human motion commands with onboard sensory feedback. We first develop a scalable terrain-aware adaptation algorithm that efficiently generates high-quality motion pairs across motions and terrains without per-motion or per-terrain tuning. Using a paired motion corpus totaling nearly 1,000 hours, we train a perceptive whole-body controller through teacher-student learning to reproduce commanded behaviors across terrains. Experiments demonstrate efficient, scalable generation of high-quality motion data and show that NEXUS combines broad behavioral coverage with terrain adaptability and tracking fidelity, outperforming existing whole-body controllers on the evaluated benchmarks. Zero-shot real-world deployment enables real-time whole-body teleoperation on diverse unseen terrains, further validating the generalization of our method. Project website: https://nexus-humanoid.github.io/

items.title: SkillBuffBench: Measuring What Agent Skills Contribute across Harnesses, Models, Skill Access Modes and Memory
items.summary: Agent Skills, file-based packages of procedural knowledge that a coding agent can discover and load on demand, are now shipped by every major agent harness, yet the evidence for how much they help comes almost entirely from settings in which the right Skill is hand-picked for the task and the agent starts from a blank slate. Neither holds in deployment, where an agent chooses from whatever library happens to be installed and frequently carries memory from earlier work. We present SkillBuffBench, a benchmark and paired evaluation protocol that treats Skill access as a three-level factor (no Skill, a curated Skill, and automatic invocation from an installed library), crosses it with memory (off and on), with four agent harnesses and with multiple models (the state-of-the-art proprietary models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI, and the state-of-the-art open-weight models from Chinese providers), every model being run under every harness, and evaluates the result on research tasks contributed by domain experts together with the Skills they use, currently in materials science and biology, with the suite extended on a rolling basis. Every run is marked by a deterministic verifier; uncertainty is reported with a paired, task-level bootstrap; and cost, agent rounds and wall-clock time are reported alongside the score rather than folded into it. This version of the paper describes the design of the benchmark, its evaluation protocol and its current tasks and Skills. The evaluation is in progress: results will be added once the runs are complete, and the task suite, results and analysis will continue to be updated on a rolling basis.

items.title: Doc-to-LoRA Analysis: Query Conditioning, Wrong Facts, and Distractor Interference
items.summary: Doc-to-LoRA (D2L) compiles documents into low-rank adapters, allowing language models to use their contents without repeatedly processing the original text. We investigate its suitability for internalizing user memories through factual question answering, controlled interventions, and a production MidBrain memory pipeline. Across Gemma-2-2B and Qwen3-4B, D2L loses accuracy relative to in-context learning, with additional documents introducing substantial interference. Single-document errors frequently match answers to other questions about the same passage, suggesting unreliable question-answer attribution. Layer-wise interventions show that interference accumulates across depth, with more concentrated early damage at larger bank sizes on Gemma. With eight documents, applying the full bank in the initial layers gives similar accuracy to withholding all document contributions there. Source membership is detectable in intermediate states, but trained readers do not reliably resolve the interference. On PersonaMem-v2, joint compilation and normalized adapter composition achieve accuracy close to consolidated text memory when retrieved episodes remain text, but the resulting token savings are modest. Measured throughput gains also depend on model and batch size despite substantial reductions in analytical compute. Together, these findings limit the practical case for D2L as a replacement for text-based memory and motivate investigating online-learning methods that acquire personalized behavior from interactions in which memory is used.

items.title: Closing the Loop: Practical Training Recipes for Looped Language Models
items.summary: Looped language models increase effective depth by repeatedly applying a shared block of layers, but existing large-scale recipes require multi-stage training over trillions of tokens, while the benefits of recurrence remain difficult to separate from differences in data and training. In this work, we establish practical training recipes for looped language models, with three main results. (1) We develop a compute-efficient from-scratch pipeline that reduces the training budget from 7.7T tokens in Ouro to 310B tokens while retaining strong reasoning performance. Pretraining followed by high-quality mid-training, together with learning-rate warmup and stronger exit-gate regularization, enables stable recurrent training without prior multi-stage schedules. (2) Under controlled comparisons, our 1.4B LoopLM outperforms a parameter-matched dense model trained on the same data and token budget on all 12 evaluated benchmarks, including +14 points on GSM8K, +10 on MATH, and +22 on DROP. At matched inference compute, it approaches a 3.9B dense model on mathematical reasoning and reading comprehension while using only 36\% as many parameters. (3) We introduce a minimal recipe for converting pretrained dense models into looped ones: a single learned input-mixing scalar and a smoothed exit loss, with no step-specific parameters. Applied to Qwen3-1.7B-Base, Looped Qwen improves over an identically continued dense baseline on every evaluated benchmark across two data regimes, with statistically clear gains on GSM8K, MATH, and MMLU-Pro on the curated mixture. Together, these results make looped language models substantially cheaper to train from scratch and practical to introduce into existing pretrained checkpoints, while isolating the gains due to recurrence itself.

items.title: Fast and Consistent Structure Learning in Graphical Models via Approximate Cross-Validation
items.summary: Structure learning for sparse graphical models in high dimensions requires both computational scalability and selection consistency. Classical criteria such as (Extended) Bayesian Information Criterion can provide consistency, but rely on model-specific likelihoods and complexity calibration. In comparison, cross-validation avoids such analytic calibration and is therefore attractive for graph learning. However, cross-validation is computationally infeasible and theoretically inconsistent in structure learning. This creates a tension between consistency and flexibility in modeling. In this work, we resolve the tension by developing a scalable graph-recovery procedure built on approximate cross-validation. We demonstrate its effectiveness in learning large graphical models both theoretically and empirically, and establish selection consistency under mild signal strength assumptions.

items.title: Ask Again: Answer-List Instability in Generative Engines
items.summary: Visibility in generative search engines is measured by which entities appear in responses, and in what order. Ask an engine the same question twice and the answer list can change: a different ordering, or different items altogether. Across 60,000 responses, we find that answers to the same prompt name a different first item 32% of the time, and even two answers with the same items disagree on which comes first. The first position is a measurement target of its own. A "clear leader" emerges after seven or eight runs, which are the budgets recommended for brand and source monitoring, but a "close leader" only about half the time. After 25 runs, a close leader is identified only 60% of the time. Variability between engines is larger than within the same engine. For open-ended prompts, the gap is more than double that for determinate ones. Search queries and cited sites observed leave most of the disagreement unexplained. Visibility measurement should report, for each engine, which items appear and how often each comes first, each with its own quantification of uncertainty.

items.title: NeuroMotion: Aligning EEG to Discrete Motion Primitives for Continuous Motion Decoding
items.summary: EEG-to-motion decoding remains challenging because noisy scalp EEG is difficult to map directly to continuous kinematics. We present NeuroMotion, a framework that aligns EEG representations to discrete motion primitives for continuous motion decoding across heterogeneous paradigms, including full-body free movement, lower-limb treadmill locomotion, and upper-limb freewill reaching and grasping. A VQ-based motion prior discretizes continuous motion into reusable primitives that serve as both alignment prototypes and intermediate prediction targets. Prototypical and supervised contrastive objectives align EEG embeddings to motion-derived prototypes and organize them according to primitive assignments. An E2M Transformer predicts motion-code sequences from the learned EEG representations, while a final geometric refinement stage improves continuous trajectory reconstruction through motion-level training. Under a last-session test protocol, NeuroMotion achieves the best mean reconstruction performance among the compared EEG decoding baselines across all three datasets, with the clearest gains on full-body motion in both reconstruction accuracy and distribution-level quality. Multi-subject ablations further support the contributions of EEG-to-primitive alignment, token prediction, and refinement. Code is available at https://github.com/Liuyi2351433/NeuroAction.

items.title: Unpacking the Evaluators: How Configuration Shapes the Evaluation of Alignment in Explainable AI
items.summary: Explainable AI (XAI) evaluation fundamentally requires human-centered evaluation, assessing whether explanations align with human reasoning and expert knowledge. However, such evaluations often require expert-driven manual validation and are difficult to scale, leading to the widespread use of alignment-based metrics, where attribution maps are compared against predefined ground-truth (GT) representations. Despite their popularity, alignment evaluations are implicitly bias towards multiple design choices made during the evaluation process, for example GT representations, metric families, metric formulations (soft vs. hard), and thresholding strategies. In this paper, we formalize alignment evaluation as a structured evaluation configuration space through which the influence of these design choices can be systematically analyzed. We further introduce a structured alignment evaluation framework that models interactions between XAI methods, GT representations, metric families, metric formulations, and thresholding strategies across 2D and 3D synthetic and real-world datasets. In addition, we propose a novel taxonomy of XAI output behavior based on local entropy and boundary mass ratio, enabling structured characterization of attribution patterns for alignment evaluation. Our experiments reveal systematic flows (triples of XAI-GT-metric configurations), showing that alignment outcomes provide distinct behavior patterns under certain configurations, such as soft/hard metric implementations. We further observe varying levels of threshold sensitivity across metric families and attribution structures. These findings demonstrate that alignment evaluation cannot be treated as a fixed or invariant measure of explanation quality, and provide practical guidance for designing more reliable and behavior-aware XAI evaluation protocols.

items.title: Asymmetric Multimodal Learning: The Alignment Redundancy Bound and Decomposed JEPAs
items.summary: Cross-modal alignment is the default objective for multimodal representation learning, but it rests on an implicit assumption: that the two modalities are roughly symmetric views of the same underlying state. We show that this assumption fails on real multimodal data, and that alignment as a sole objective is provably lossy under informational asymmetry. We formalize the failure through Partial Information Decomposition, proving that cross-modal alignment retains at most the redundant information atom and annihilates the modality-unique and synergistic structure on which asymmetric tasks depend. We give the exact PID decomposition of the alignment information bottleneck, characterize its failure regime, and derive a sufficiency condition that any encoder objective must satisfy to preserve all four informational atoms. We then introduce Decomposed JEPA (D-JEPA), which realizes this condition by factorizing each modality's latent space into an aligned shared core and a private fiber anchored by contextual masked prediction. On compositional reasoning benchmarks, alignment-only training undergoes catastrophic semantic collapse on relational queries; D-JEPA prevents this collapse, recovering the referent structure alignment discards, restoring most of the mutual information available from a frozen backbone, and producing positive multimodal synergy where alignment inverts it. Information-theoretic and causal audits confirm that the recovered information is causally localized in the private fibers.

items.title: Which $\Diamond \mathcal{P}$ Algorithm is Suitable for You? An Empirical Benchmark on Real Network Traces
items.summary: Unreliable failure detectors (UFDs) are a fundamental abstraction for dependability and fault tolerance in distributed systems, supporting core distributed algorithms, such as consensus. Yet selecting a suitable detector remains difficult because existing implementations are evaluated under different environments, workloads, parameterizations, and quality-of-service (QoS) requirements. We address this problem by systematizing 14 $\Diamond \mathcal{P}$ and closely related $\Diamond \mathcal{P}$-style UFDs, implementing 13 of them, and providing a reusable benchmark for their empirical comparison. Our methodology evaluates detectors through common QoS metrics, such as detection time, mistake rate, and query accuracy, and combines same-input replay of network traces with live deployment for detectors whose active probing or cooperative behavior requires online execution. We then formalize failure-detector selection as a constrained algorithm-selection challenge, mapping operational requirements to suitable detector candidates. We instantiate this methodology under controlled variations of communication rate, host load, and crash regime. Applying the selection process shows that no detector is uniformly preferable across the evaluated settings. At relaxed detection-time budgets, 2W [Tomsic et al., IPDPS 2015] is the most frequently selected detector, appearing in 12 of 16 scenario-metric combinations for $T_D \le 500$ ms, whereas stricter budgets yield substantially more scenario- and metric-dependent selections. The benchmark and selection methodology provide a reusable basis for practical detector selection and for establishing stronger analytical baselines for future failure-detection approaches, including learning-based detectors.

items.title: HIVE-Bench: Evaluating Patch-Level Visual Representations for Egocentric Robot Manipulation
items.summary: Pretrained vision is a common start for robot learning, but most comparisons still score one pooled vector from a third-person image. Bimanual policies instead read dense patch tokens from cameras on the robot. We introduce HIVE-Bench: one shared flow-matching policy reads 20 encoders from seven families on 24 egocentric bimanual tasks, across adaptation, task sharing, and sweeps of data, model size, and layer. Keeping the patches matters. Averaging each view to one token removes most of the success, adaptation helps every pair we test, and one shared policy keeps most of the success of separate policies at a fraction of the updates. The same tokens are then scored with statistics, state and object readouts, published vision scores, and an inverse-dynamics readout. That readout of the commanded motion is one of the strongest measurements available before a policy is trained. Recognition, depth, and correspondence do not transfer reliably. Fine-tuning can improve the action readout even when other measurements move the other way, and no statistic is stable enough to replace a rollout before any deployment.

items.title: Support-Constrained Local Randomizers for Robust Private Distribution Learning
items.summary: Local differential privacy protects users before data collection, but full-support randomizers can be wasteful on ordered, metric, or semantic alphabets. We study support-constrained local randomizers for robust private discrete learning. Restricting reports to input neighborhoods reduces reporting distortion but creates support mismatch. Under range-restricted approximate local differential privacy, a relational guarantee weaker than ordinary all-pairs local differential privacy, we decompose the exact hockey-stick defect into support leakage and overlap excess loss. For line-supported sparse randomized response, we derive the exact defect, solve the joint privacy-distortion problem in closed form at each radius, and prove a privacy-imposed support lower bound. For distribution estimation, we obtain an exact finite-sample risk identity and show that the least-favorable law over any closed convex uncertainty set is a Euclidean projection. On cyclic alphabets, the uniform law is uniquely least favorable, nominal and minimax mechanism rankings coincide, and the minimax risk obeys spectral upper and lower bounds. This diagnoses why prior shift cannot alter the selected mechanism in a homogeneous cyclic experiment. We therefore introduce a boundary-normalized nonhomogeneous path family in which robust calibration changes the mechanism and reduces worst-case risk. We also derive exact cyclic privacy, robust privacy-range calibration, and precise conditions for safe context- or history-dependent channel selection. Sparse Laplace, Gaussian, staircase, and score-based mechanisms remain extensions of the same design principle. All numerical results use exact privacy and risk calculations with matched-guarantee baselines.

items.title: Characterizing normality via automata and random matrix products
items.summary: For a fixed alphabet A, an infinite sequence X is said to be normal if every word w over A appears in X with the same frequency as any other word of the same length. A classical result relates normality to finite automata as follows: a sequence X is normal if and only if all gambling strategies implementable with finite deterministic automata lose all their capital when trying to predict the next bit of X after seing the ones before. More precisely, Schnorr and Stimm (1972) proved that the capital goes exponentially fast to zero unless the automaton represents the gambler that never bets, in which case the capital remains constant. In this paper we show that an analogous result holds when considering probabilistic automata: a sequence X is normal if and only if for any gambling strategy implementable with probabilistic finite automaton it holds that the expected value of the capital of the gambler converges exponentially fast to a finite value when playing against X. To obtain this result, we show a more general statement related to the convergence of martingales given by finite sets of non-negative matrices {M a } a$\in$A . In particular, we show that X is normal if and only if ||vM X[1] . . . M X[n] || converges exponentially fast to a finite value for any non-negative starting vector v. Moreover, we distinguish three distinctive behaviours that this sequence can attain, and prove that the problem of recognizing, given a family of matrices, to which case it belongs, is decidable.

items.title: PPGFlowECG: Latent Rectified Flow with Cross-Modal Encoding for PPG-Guided ECG Generation and Cardiovascular Disease Detection
items.summary: Electrocardiography (ECG) is the clinical gold standard for cardiovascular disease (CVD) assessment, yet continuous monitoring is constrained by the need for dedicated hardware and trained personnel. Photoplethysmography (PPG) is ubiquitous in wearable devices and readily scalable, but it lacks electrophysiological specificity, limiting diagnostic reliability. While generative methods aim to translate PPG into clinically useful ECG signals, existing approaches are limited by the misalignment of physiological semantics in generative models and the complexity of modeling in high-dimensional signals. To address these limitations, we propose PPGFlowECG, a two-stage framework that aligns PPG and ECG in a shared latent space using the CardioAlign Encoder and then synthesizes ECGs with latent rectified flow. We further provide a formal analysis of this coupling, showing that the CardioAlign Encoder is necessary to guarantee stable and semantically consistent ECG synthesis under our formulation. Extensive experiments on four datasets demonstrate improved synthesis fidelity and downstream diagnostic utility. These results indicate that PPGFlowECG supports scalable, wearable-first CVD screening when standard ECG acquisition is unavailable.

items.title: Go Far, Look Less: Active Multi-Room Reconstruction with Persistent Goals and Selective Views
items.summary: Active 3D reconstruction aims to allocate a sparse view budget to recover complete geometry and high-fidelity renderings. However, existing methods degrade sharply in multi-room homes: myopic next-best-view scoring gives transit no credit for distant rooms and over-polishes irreducible nearby residuals, whereas dense mappers reach far rooms only by streaming thousands of frames. We propose ROAM-GS, a training-free active multi-room reconstruction framework that couples persistent goals with selective views: each decision selects a goal and a variable-horizon prefix toward it, capturing only at its endpoint. A Surface Reconstruction Memory scores poses by projecting post-update defects and viewing directions. Persistent goals credit transit with their remaining value and are released once arrivals stop measurably improving them. Without per-scene tuning, ROAM-GS achieves state-of-the-art multi-room reconstruction while preserving single-room Replica fidelity, raising mean coverage from 74% to 93% on HSSD and from 47% to 96% (+11.7 dB PSNR) on HM3D, and matching 90-minute dense mapping using $173\times$ fewer views.

items.title: Big Tree Viewer: A high-performance browser-based phylogenetic tree viewer with agentic AI integration
items.summary: Phylogenetic trees represent evolutionary history visually, and the ability to display and explore them is a key function in research across biological disciplines. Very large gene and species trees are becoming common with the increasing availability of low cost DNA sequencing, creating performance and informativeness challenges for display software originally designed for phylogenies with a few hundred to a few thousand tips. We discuss these limitations and introduce a browser-based Big Tree Viewer (BTV) highly optimized for fast display and biologically informative exploration of phylogenetic trees containing even a million tips. BTV can automatically map binomial species names to the NCBI or Catalogue of Life taxonomies and display colored ribbons to indicate taxonomic groups for enhanced exploration. Even without taxonomic mapping, BTV automatically labels groups of neighboring tips that share the first word of their names, such as a genus or gene family name, providing readable large-scale landmarks when individual tip labels are too dense to read. BTV supports metadata display, visual customization, tanglegram-like tree comparisons, statistics, figure export, and multiple tree layouts, including a new spiral form to display enormously large trees. BTV is also designed to integrate with common agentic AI tools, allowing agents to display, style, annotate, and inspect trees at the user's request. The BTV web app is freely available at https://BigTreeViewer.net and runs entirely in the user's browser, with no data uploads to any central server. Desktop versions of the BTV app for macOS, Windows, and Linux are also provided for download.

items.title: On the interpretation of the kinetics of ligand-receptor binding
items.summary: When the rates of ligand binding are measured by methods such as surface plasmon resonance, it is common practice to use the observed rate constants for the onset and offset of binding to estimate an equilibrium constant for ligand binding. If this agrees with the equilibrium constant found as the EC50 for binding at equilibrium, this is taken as validation of the measured rates. This is correct only when binding produces no conformation change in the receptor, and ligand binding follows a single exponential time course. Here, we investigate a simple 3 state model in which binding is followed by a conformation change in the receptor. Three special cases of this model in which the time course of onset and offset of ligand binding are close to being single exponentials are analysed. These cases are (1) when binding is much faster than the conformation change, (2) when the conformation change is much faster than binding, and (3) when the rates of ligand dissociation and receptor activation are both fast. It is concluded that the measured rates will often yield an estimate of the equilibrium constant for ligand binding that is close to the effective, or macroscopic, equilibrium constant, the EC50 found by measuring binding at equilibrium, which depends on both of the underlying microscopic equilibrium constants describing ligand binding and the conformation change. The exception to this conclusion is the case when binding is much faster than the subsequent conformation change, though the estimate of the equilibrium constant for ligand binding still depends on both of the underlying microscopic equilibrium constants.

items.title: From Organization to Viability: A Multi-Level Analysis of Gait Dynamics Under Occlusal Constraint
items.summary: Clinical interpretation often assumes that observable performance sufficiently reflects the organization of an adaptive system. The preceding Level 3 study showed that neither an aggregated scalar score nor a static exploratory UMAP embedding uniquely resolved the occlusal observational probes. This study introduces Level 4, centered on observed longitudinal viability. Using an exploratory single-case design in a participant with Parkinson's disease, gait was recorded with instrumented insoles under three probes: neutral natural occlusion (ONL), a nominal 2.5-degree increase in vertical dimension of occlusion (OC2.5), and a nominal 3-degree increase (OC3). Two sessions were conducted eleven weeks apart. A common PCA representation was used to compare M1-M2 centroid displacement. In the selected PC1-PC2 plane, OC3 showed the smallest Euclidean displacement, ONL an intermediate displacement, and OC2.5 the largest. This ordering was preserved in most bootstrap iterations but was not preserved after Mahalanobis covariance normalization, showing that within-condition dispersion contributes to the result. Level 4 therefore provides a retrospective, representation-dependent proxy for longitudinal reorganization when static representations remain non-identifying. The findings are exploratory and non-causal. They do not establish distinct physiological states, a causal occlusal effect, a validated viability threshold, a therapeutic optimum, or a covariance-independent ranking.

items.title: Boosting Brain-to-Image Decoding with TRIBE v2 Data Augmentation
items.summary: Brain decoding is limited by the availability of labeled neural data, and remains challenging in low-data regimes. To address this issue, we investigate whether and when brain decoding can be boosted by augmenting small fMRI datasets with synthetic data generated by a pretrained model of fMRI responses to stimuli. We use TRIBE v2, a large encoding model pretrained on more than 1000 hours of fMRI responses to video, audio and language. For each dataset, we evaluate systematic grids that show how the performance of image decoders varies with the amount of synthetic data used for training. Our results, based on two datasets (the 7T fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset and 3T fMRI BOLD5000), show up to 68% improvement in Top-10 image-retrieval accuracy compared to decoders trained only on real data. Importantly, the proportion of augmented data required to reach a given image decoding performance needs to be adjusted depending on the data source. Surprisingly, image decoders trained exclusively on synthetic fMRI can perform above chance in some settings, suggesting that TRIBE v2 can support zero-shot brain-to-image decoding. Together, these results show how large-scale models of the fMRI responses to sight, sound and language may provide a foundation to improve the data efficiency for image decoding.

items.title: From joint attention to shared symbols: A free-energy principle account
items.summary: Joint attention precedes vocabulary acquisition. How can attending to the same object help two people with different sensory experiences come to use a shared word? In a free-energy principle account, marginalizing the common object induces a statistical dependence between private perceptual states. In a categorical world, the joint prior inherits a mixture structure whose component index provides a candidate for shared reference. The collective predictive coding model approximates this prior by representing the dependence through that shared index. An established Metropolis-Hastings naming game lets agents infer and exchange words using private evidence. Toy and multiview image experiments illustrate how word exchange can coordinate private categories and improve the fit of collective models. The account connects joint attention to shared symbols through the coupling of private inference.

items.title: Comparison of 3D-DXA Measurements with QCT Software Solutions for Proximal Femur Bone Density Assessment
items.summary: 3D-Shaper reconstructs proximal femur shape and density in 3D from a standard hip dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) scan. In men and women aged 35-91 years, we compared 3D-Shaper integral volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD), trabecular vBMD, and cortical surface BMD (sBMD) with quantitative computed tomography (QCT) processed with three methods: an in-house pipeline, Stradview and QCTPro CTXA, which were used to derive bone measurements equivalent to those of 3D-Shaper. Agreement, including among QCT methods, was assessed with linear regression and Bland-Altman analysis (bias and limits of agreement, LoA). 3D-Shaper agreed strongly with the in-house pipeline and Stradview for integral vBMD (R=0.95-0.96; bias 1.5 to 4.2 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$39.7 to 41.4 mg/cm$^3$), trabecular vBMD (R=0.92-0.94; bias -11.8 to -7.8 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$33.3 to 39.4 mg/cm$^3$) and cortical sBMD (R=0.94; bias 5.6 to 38.2 mg/cm$^2$; LoA $\pm$23.6 to 26.4 mg/cm$^2$). The in-house pipeline and Stradview agreed for integral vBMD (R=1.00; bias -2.7 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$3.7 mg/cm$^3$), trabecular vBMD (R=0.96-1.00; bias -0.2 to 3.9 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$6.9 to 27.5 mg/cm$^3$) and cortical sBMD (R=0.98; bias 32.7 mg/cm$^2$; LoA $\pm$14.6 mg/cm$^2$). Compared with 3D-Shaper, QCTPro CTXA integral vBMD was systematically lower (R=0.90; bias -28.4 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$61.5 mg/cm$^3$) and trabecular vBMD showed a proportional bias (R=0.89; bias -44.1 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$61.3 mg/cm$^3$). The same pattern was observed against the other QCT methods, for integral vBMD (R=0.93; bias -32.6 to -29.9 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$49.6 to 50.0 mg/cm$^3$) and trabecular vBMD (R=0.94-0.96; bias -36.3 to -32.5 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$51.2 to 54.9 mg/cm$^3$). These findings support the agreement of 3D-Shaper with independent QCT approaches and show that 3D-Shaper-QCT differences must be interpreted in light of the QCT method used.

items.title: PlainMap: a lightweight, restartable mapping pipeline for ancient and modern DNA
items.summary: Mapping sequencing reads to a reference genome requires preprocessing and alignment choices that can vary with library type, fragment length, sequencing platform, and reference genome. These considerations are particularly important for ancient and historical DNA, where short and damaged fragments complicate read mapping. We present PlainMap, a lightweight and restartable mapping pipeline for modern and degraded DNA sequencing data. PlainMap accepts a simple manifest of FASTQ files, identifies single-end and paired-end data from read headers, supports heterogeneous sequencing inputs, and provides alternative mapping strategies for modern and degraded DNA. Optional pilot subsampling allows users to rapidly compare mapped fragment recovery across different settings using identical subsets of raw data, without attempting to determine the most accurate mapping strategy. Chunking and checkpoint-based execution support processing large datasets and resuming interrupted analyses, allowing users to balance memory requirements, runtime, and restartability. PlainMap produces duplicate-filtered BAM files together with fragment-aware mapping and coverage statistics. Evaluation using heterogeneous Japanese sea lion and short-fragment cave hyena datasets demonstrated successful processing across mapping modes, consistent trimmed and merged read counts across chunk sizes, and recovery from interrupted analyses without repeating completed mapping steps. PlainMap is implemented as a single Bash script and is freely available at https://github.com/BiodiversityExtinction/PlainMap.

items.title: VCBench: Benchmarking virtual cell models for in-the-wild perturbation response
items.summary: Virtual cell (VC) models aim to predict cellular responses to diverse perturbations in silico, offering great promise for drug discovery and precision medicine. However, although models routinely report strong performance on existing benchmarks, whether these predictions translate to practical biological utility remains unclear. Current evaluations often rely on overly simplified or inconsistent setups that fail to capture the complexity and variability of real biological systems. Here, we present a standardized, modular benchmarking framework that evaluates nine VC models under challenging, in-the-wild scenarios spanning unseen cell lines and donors, novel genetic and chemical perturbations, and cross-study transfer. Across these evaluations, complex models do not consistently surpass simple linear baselines on broad transcriptional trends, while fine-grained, perturbation-specific effects remain difficult to recover. Moreover, different evaluation metrics emphasize distinct biological properties, resulting in markedly different model rankings. Consequently, model selection and data integration strategies should be tailored to specific downstream tasks rather than applied uniformly. Together, this framework establishes a more biologically grounded benchmark to guide model development, evaluation, and deployment in real-world settings.

items.title: Learning Multimodal Representations from Partially Paired, Small-Scale Data
items.summary: Modeling multimodal data from partially paired samples is critical for advancing domains like biomedicine, where vast unimodal datasets and foundation models exist but paired data remains scarce. Existing fusion methods rely on large-scale paired datasets, limiting their use in scenarios with incomplete pairing. We introduce CAMEO, an adversarial learning-based modality fusion framework that integrates modalities from small, partially paired datasets. Combining any pre-trained unimodal encoder with a cross-modal latent alignment mechanism, CAMEO learns shared representations requiring only minimal paired samples. Evaluated on computational pathology tasks such as niche classification and cell type composition prediction, CAMEO achieves superior data efficiency, outperforming contrastive approaches like CLIP in low paired-data regimes, and highlighting the benefits of adversarial alignment when paired annotations are scarce. To facilitate further research, we additionally release a fully annotated HuggingFace dataset comprising three organs and paired image and gene expression modalities. By extending fusion methods to address limited pairing and small-scale datasets, we provide a framework that advances multimodal learning and broadens its applicability to real-world biomedical problems.

items.title: Beyond the Blueprint: The Continuing Evolution of Turing's Theory of Morphogenesis
items.summary: Turing's article ``The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis'' has profoundly influenced conceptual views on the emergence of biological form across scales and species. It has also served as a foundational framework to guide experimental investigations into the mechanisms that underlie pattern formation. In this article, we trace the historical development of Turing's ideas and examine their integration into contemporary research programs. We critically assess the broad and often overlapping concepts that have derived from Turing's work, both highlighting value in productive applications of the theory and suggesting that skepticism should remain in overly simplistic validations. By clarifying these concepts and their intrinsic limitations, we rethink contemporary approaches aimed at understanding the essential principles that govern biological pattern formation. We pose some important challenges that will require interdisciplinary expertise to overcome, and which will necessitate fundamentally new paradigms to understand the physical origin of Darwin's ``endless forms most beautiful''.

items.title: Pesticide mixtures may compromise ecosystem services provided by an egg parasitoid of soybean pest stink bugs: a comprehensive ecotoxicological risk assessment
items.summary: Tank mixtures of crop protection products are widely used in agricultural systems, yet their integrated effects on biological control agents remain poorly understood. We evaluated the lethal, sublethal, and transgenerational effects of four synthetic insecticides, applied alone or in binary mixtures with three fungicides and two herbicides, on adults and pupae of Telenomus podisi (Hymenoptera: Scelionidae), an important egg parasitoid of pest stink bugs. In adult bioassays, LC50 values ranged from 28.26 mg a.i. L-1 for isocycloseram + lambda-cyhalothrin to 265.88 mg a.i. L-1 for acephate. Overall, mixtures increased adverse effects relative to the individual products, reducing survival, parasitism, and longevity. The lowest parasitism rates occurred with isocycloseram + lambda-cyhalothrin combined with chlorothalonil or glyphosate SL formulation. Transgenerational effects were also detected, including reduced F1 emergence and an increased proportion of males in some treatments. Following pupal exposure, several mixtures reduced F0 emergence, whereas ethiprole + fenpropimorph and acephate + bixafen + prothioconazole + trifloxystrobin also reduced parasitism and longevity of the emerged adults. Integration of lethal and sublethal responses using the reduction coefficient (Ex) revealed increased toxicity for several mixtures and shifts in IOBC risk classification; notably, all insecticide + glyphosate mixtures reached Ex = 100% after pupal exposure. These findings show that assessing pesticides individually may underestimate ecotoxicological risk to T. podisi and highlight the need to consider pesticide mixtures in integrated pest management programs.

items.title: Interactions with hidden traits induce diversification and conceal its origin
items.summary: Adaptive diversification is often inferred from a small number of measurable traits, even though evolutionary dynamics arise from many interacting phenotypic dimensions. Unmeasured traits may therefore do more than bias inference: through their interactions, they may determine whether diversification occurs at all. Here we develop a theory of the onset and attribution of adaptive diversification by partitioning phenotype space into focal and hidden sectors. Eliminating the hidden sector yields an exact effective operator. Coupling to hidden traits that are stabilizing in isolation can destabilize an otherwise stable phenotype and generate a diversifying composite mode: the interaction creates diversification rather than merely strengthening it. Conversely, when the hidden sector is itself diversifying, the focal traits diversify as a correlated response to a hidden-driven process: no effective description in the focal traits, not even the exact one obtained by eliminating the hidden sector, predicts the variation they display, and stabilizing the focal traits reduces it without removing it. These effects become strongest near the hidden sector's own threshold, so a weakly stabilized hidden trait can have a large effect even with modest coupling to the focal traits, and they can generate correlations between focal traits that have no direct interaction. Onset and observability are distinct: systems with the same leading eigenvalue can project very differently onto the measured traits, so the theory tracks both the full operator and the focal-hidden partition. Individual-based simulations recover the predicted threshold and variance law, coupling-induced trait splitting, and the reversal of induced correlations. Interactions with unmeasured traits can both create adaptive diversification and determine whether the diversification seen in measured phenotypes can be attributed to them.

items.title: From Clever Hans to Hypotheses: Interpreting EEG Foundational Transformers with LRP
items.summary: Emerging foundation models (FMs) in electroencephalography (EEG) promise a path to scale deep learning in diagnostics and brain-computer interfaces despite data scarcity, yet their opaque nature remains a barrier to wider adoption. We investigate attention-aware Layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) as a post-hoc attribution method for EEG-FMs, extending LRP's use on convolutional neural network (CNN)-based EEG models to the Transformer architectures that current FMs are based on. We find that LRP can both verify EEG-FM decisions and surface novel, biologically plausible hypotheses from them. In motor imagery, it unmasks 'Clever Hans' behavior where models prioritize task correlated ocular signals over the intended motor correlates. In a naturalistic paradigm for affect prediction, it reveals a recurring reliance on a central electrode cluster, suggesting a candidate sensorimotor signature of arousal. Though heatmap interpretation remains ambiguous in this complex domain, the results position LRP as a tool for both verification and exploration of EEG-FMs, a role that will grow in both importance and discovery potential as the underlying models mature.

items.title: Emergent self-inhibition governs the landscape of stable states in complex ecosystems
items.summary: Species-rich ecosystems often exhibit multiple stable states with distinct species compositions. Yet, the factors determining the likelihood of each state's occurrence remain poorly understood. Here, we characterize and explain the landscape of stable states in the random Generalized Lotka--Volterra (GLV) model, in which multistability is widespread. We focus on the regime of the model where interspecies interactions are predominantly competitive and nearly symmetric. We find that the same pool of species with random initial abundances can result in different stable states, whose likelihoods typically differ by orders of magnitude. A state's likelihood increases sharply with its total biomass, or inverse self-inhibition. We develop a simplified model to predict and explain this behavior, by coarse-graining ecological interactions so that each stable state behaves as a unit. In this setting, we can accurately predict the entire landscape of stable states using only two macroscopic properties: the biomass of each state and species diversity. Our analyses also provide insight into the biomass--likelihood relationship: High-biomass states have low self-inhibition and thus grow faster, outcompete others, and become much more likely. These results reveal emergent self-inhibition as a fundamental organizing principle for the attractor landscape of complex ecosystems---and provide a path to predict ecosystem outcomes without knowing microscopic interactions.

items.title: Katz Kernel Based Stratification of Breast Cancer Patients
items.summary: The integration of mechanistic signaling networks into clinical research has become a cornerstone of precision oncology. By capturing the complex biochemical interactions within a cell, these networks provide a functional map of disease progression that goes beyond simple genomic mutations. Consequently, the development of specific signaling models of patients has significant relevance, allowing for a more granular representation of individual disease profiles. In this setting, there is a growing need for robust methodologies capable of comparing graph based pathway structures to identify similarities and differences across patient cohorts. Such comparisons are essential for the identification of clinically meaningful subgroups, and the discovery of novel biomarkers. Standard graph kernels, while mathematically rigorous, often remain too generic for this purpose. They frequently fail to capture features specific to gene signaling networks, resulting in suboptimal clustering performance. In this paper, we present a domain specific graph kernel designed for mechanistic signaling networks. Unlike generic approaches, our method explicitly incorporates biological constraints and gene interaction patterns into the kernel formulation, enabling a more accurate characterization of both topological structure and functional behavior. We assess its performance on breast cancer datasets, focusing on its ability to support disease subtyping. Our results suggest that our approach can effectively contribute to patient stratification.

items.title: Fluctuating resource availability stabilizes coexistence beyond the oscillatory tragedy of the commons
items.summary: Fluctuations in ambient conditions such as temperature and humidity can alter the effective availability of a shared resource at a given abundance. Standard evolutionary games with environmental feedback treat the payoff matrix as a deterministic function of resource abundance, leaving open how fluctuations in availability affect the oscillatory tragedy of the commons. Using noise-corrected replicator dynamics and individual-based birth-death simulations, we show that zero-mean fluctuations in resource availability can stabilize an interior equilibrium and suppress coupled strategy-resource oscillations. We derive an analytical criterion, in terms of the payoff structure and feedback dynamics, for when increasing noise favors local stability. These findings identify environmental variability as a mechanism that can promote strategy coexistence and help maintain shared resources in systems prone to recurrent depletion.

items.title: Old Matches, New Frames: Schedule-Gated Stereo Memory from Human Vision to Machine Matching
items.summary: Human vision and video stereo networks both reuse disparity evidence across time, yet a refresh of the input can invalidate a match formed milliseconds earlier. What tells a system whether an old match still counts? We answer this from limited human data in three steps. First, nine temporal mechanisms share a frozen binocular-energy front end and an equal-capacity readout, so held-out behavior isolates the temporal selection rule: on 240 conditions from 10 observers, down-weighting aged evidence that has lost binocular support lowers subject RMSE from 12.6% to 10.3% and reproduces a period-dependent reversed-depth illusion, across all 59 readings of the unpublished protocol and 8 front-end perturbations. Second, four propositions establish what such data can identify: gating is identified at the level of the refresh schedule, and candidate binding is invisible to standard stimuli but exposed by a single-eye geometry flip that separates the readouts by up to 7.1%. Third, the identified rule becomes a two-field stereo memory that separates sample validity from hypothesis support. It removes a 50 ms recovery lag after geometry flips, and its regime analysis explains why plain integration stays preferable on MPI-Sintel, where 71.1% of pixels change appearance but not disparity.

items.title: Hierarchical Hybrid-Coordinate Flow Matching for Accurate and Physically Plausible Apo-to-Holo Protein Generation
items.summary: Predicting holo-like protein conformations from apo structures is essential in structure-based drug design. Most existing apo-to-holo models operate in Cartesian space and achieve strong global accuracy. However, high global accuracy does not ensure physically valid local backbone geometry. Internal-coordinate models offer local control and validity, but regressive generation can amplify angular errors, known as the lever-arm effect. We introduce CrypticFlow, a hierarchical flow-matching model that combines these two complementary representations. An ESM-3-conditioned E(3)-equivariant graph network first generates sparse C$α$ anchors in Cartesian space. A conditional midpoint Transformer then recursively fills the gaps in local internal coordinates. During recursive generation, the decoder constrains the distance between each midpoint and any sequence-adjacent parent anchor to the corresponding apo C$α$-C$α$ distance. On the D3PM test split, CrypticFlow achieves the lowest median and mean C$α$ RMSD at published baseline capacities. Across five independent training models, the median and mean direct RMSD are 1.333 $\pm$ 0.056 angstroms and 2.766 $\pm$ 0.041 angstroms, respectively. The quality of local geometry also improves substantially. Our model achieves 99.58 $\pm$ 0.02% adjacent-distance fidelity and 95.87 $\pm$ 0.25% pseudo-angle fidelity, measured within 0.2 angstroms and 20° of the holo reference. Then, we reconstruct the predicted C$α$-only traces into all-atom structures using the cg2all coarse-to-all-atom backmapping method and evaluate their physical and geometric quality with MolProbity. Our model achieves a MolProbity score of 3.034 $\pm$ 0.054, outperforming the evaluated baselines. These results show that a hierarchical flow-matching model with hybrid coordinates can recover global accuracy while retaining local fidelity.

items.title: Separating Genetic and Protein Evidence in Open Targets: An Auditable Re-ranking Study
items.summary: Biomedical target-ranking platforms combine genetics, literature, experimental evidence, tractability, and clinical precedent because each is useful for target discovery. A single integrated score, however, can be awkward to reuse for a narrower question such as which genes have direct evidence for disease risk or etiology. We examine this issue in Open Targets associations for Alzheimer disease (AD) and Parkinson disease (PD). Genetics-linked evidence and protein-oriented evidence are scored in separate channels and combined only at the end. In AD, the Open Targets overall top 20 contains 7 curated genetics-supported genes and 10 symptomatic pharmacology controls; the default late fusion contains 15 curated genes and no symptomatic controls. In PD, late fusion retains 13 curated genes and removes the 5 symptomatic controls present in the platform top 20. A genetics-only ranking reaches similar curated recall (14 genes in AD, 13 in PD), so most of the gain over the platform score comes from emphasizing genetic evidence; the protein channel mainly raises the number of tractable targets in the shortlist (from 9 to 12 in AD and from 8 to 10 in PD) without readmitting symptomatic controls. These results are stable across fusion weights from 0.35 to 0.75, perturbed protein-channel weights, and rule thresholds. An optional post-ranking rule further lowers high-clinical/low-genetic targets such as ACHE and GRIN1 without changing top-20 curated recall. The procedure is deterministic and uses public Open Targets fields. Because the component scores remain available, individual rank changes can be inspected and the ranking can be reproduced from the same data snapshot.

items.title: GABIF: An Adaptive Guided Graph Denoising Framework for Antibody Conditional Inverse Folding
items.summary: Antibodies play a central role in the human immune system, and their design is critical for vaccine development, therapeutic intervention, and improving human longevity. However, the vast combinatorial search space of antibodies poses a fundamental challenge for de novo discovery. Recent advances in deep learning, particularly denoising diffusion models, have demonstrated strong potential in protein inverse folding. Nevertheless, existing approaches are largely constrained to learning from natural antibody repertoires, thereby generating sequences that closely resemble natural antibodies. Such similarity, however, does not necessarily translate into improved functional performance in downstream applications. In this work, we develop a novel generative protein design model that enables the generation and optimization of antibody sequences tailored to specific downstream tasks and target metrics. Besides training on given an antibody dataset, we guide the generative model by an antibody-antigen binding affinity predictor for conditional discrete diffusion. The model is pre-trained on a given antibody dataset. Meanwhile, an antibody-antigen binding affinity predictor is incorporated as a conditional signal in a discrete diffusion framework, where a regressor serves as the conditional probability to guide the learning of the amino acid probability distribution of sequences under the objective of affinity optimization. In silico experiments demonstrate that our antibody design model achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art approaches, while the proposed regressor effectively improves binding affinity, as validated by an independent external predictor. Furthermore, our results highlight that the combination of finetuning and supervised guidance provides a powerful paradigm for adapting pretrained models to downstream tasks.

items.title: Stationary covariance spectra of discrete-time non-normal random recurrent dynamics
items.summary: Principal component analysis is widely used to characterize structure in the dynamics of recurrent neural networks. For stationary noise-driven dynamics, the distribution of variance among the principal components is determined by the spectrum of the stationary covariance matrix. While the spectral properties of this matrix are well-understood for linear networks with normal synaptic weight matrices, our understanding of the stationary covariance spectrum for random non-normal dynamics remains incomplete. In this note, we use a free-probability approach to show almost-sure convergence of the stationary covariance spectrum of discrete-time dynamics with random non-normal Gaussian weights, and derive a closed functional equation characterizing its distribution.
