The proposed framework develops temporal baselines with ARIMA models, applies an NNGP correction to residual spatial dependencies and then combines the two components to produce improved forecasts. RMSE of the hybrid model is reduced by 17.4% (1.416 vs 1.715 m/s) compared to ARIMA baseline (station-wise improvements up to 48.9%); rolling-origin forecast evaluation over five origins with ten-day horizon was used (spatial correlation range = 103km, temporal persistence = 0.46), blockwise conformal prediction intervals cover 99.5% and Diebold-Mariano tests show statistical significance of improvements (DM = 6.44, p < 0.001). Spatial dependencies should be accounted for in temporal forecasting to improve prediction accuracy, especially at high-elevation stations, where spatial effects are strongest.

items.title: How many mistakes does it take to learn an interval? Exact Littlestone dimensions of intervals and their unions
items.summary: The Littlestone dimension of a hypothesis class equals the smallest number of mistakes an online learner can guarantee against an adaptive adversary. For discrete intervals and unions of $j$ intervals on $m$ points, only its order of growth was known. We determine it exactly. For every switch budget $k$ (with both end labels fixed when $k$ is odd), the smallest size on which $d$ mistakes can be forced follows a three-regime law: $d+1$ while $d\le k$, then $2d-k+1$, and beyond $d=\lceil 3k/2\rceil+k-1$ doubling the size adds exactly $k$ mistakes. Unions of $j$ intervals on $m$ points correspond to $k=2j$ and size $m+1$, and a single interval gives the thresholds $1,2,3,5,7,10,14,20,\dots$. The natural learner that waits for a positive example and binary-searches both endpoints is not optimal: it can be forced into one extra mistake for 50,847 of the domain sizes below $10^5$. Upper bounds come from a gap potential and a block-pairing learner, and lower bounds from adversary strategies and a refinement step. These tools give an explicit optimal learner with $O(\log m)$ time per round, which on random streams makes more mistakes on average than the natural learner. For randomised learners, we compute the randomised Littlestone dimension of thresholds exactly and prove that a greedy adversary forces an explicit closed-form number of expected mistakes on intervals; this bound is within $0.64$ of optimal and, we conjecture, exact (confirmed for $m\le70$). Exact computation tests every result, and the formulas for every switch budget are machine-checked in Lean 4.

items.title: Conformal prediction for high-dimensional functional time series: Applications to subnational mortality
items.summary: In statistics, forecast uncertainty is often quantified using a specified statistical model, though such approaches may be vulnerable to model misspecification, selection bias, and limited finite-sample validity. While bootstrap procedures may alleviate some of these concerns, their validity is not guaranteed and they are often computationally demanding. Instead, we take a model-agnostic and distribution-free approach, namely conformal prediction, to construct pointwise prediction intervals in high-dimensional functional time series. Among a rich family of conformal prediction methods, we study split, non-conformity score, sequential predictive, and adaptive conformal prediction. In split and non-conformity score conformal prediction, the data are divided into training, validation, and test sets, and the interval width is calibrated on the validation set so that the empirical coverage probability matches the nominal level, by tuning a coefficient of the residual standard deviation and by taking an empirical quantile of the non-conformity scores, respectively. Sequential predictive conformal prediction removes the need for a validation set by updating predictive quantiles sequentially via an autoregressive process, whereas adaptive conformal prediction updates the significance level over time according to the coverage of past intervals. Using subnational age- and sex-specific $\log$ mortality data from Japan and Canada, we compare the finite-sample forecast performance of the conformal prediction methods considered, using empirical coverage probability and the mean interval score.

items.title: Hierarchical Bayesian Estimation of Covariance Matrices
items.summary: We develop a hierarchical Bayesian framework for covariance matrix estimation built on a key observation: while equivariance under the full general linear group GL(p) is well known, it is an extremely restrictive property. Estimators equivariant to GL(p) are limited to scalar multiples of the sample covariance matrix and carry considerably larger risks than shrinkage estimators. By contrast, commonly used shrinkage estimators, including the Haff empirical Bayes estimator and the Ledoit-Wolf estimators, are all equivariant under the smaller orthogonal group O(p). Exploiting this structure, we establish that the Haar measure Bayes rule in an oracle eigenvalue model is the minimum risk estimator within the class of O(p)-equivariant estimators, and derive oracle Bayes rules for the covariance and precision matrices under the squared Frobenius, Stein, and squared Stein loss functions. These oracle rules serve as theoretical benchmarks for all O(p)-equivariant estimators. To approximate them when the true eigenvalues are unknown, we introduce a hierarchical Bayes model that places a finite Pólya tree prior on the eigenvalue distribution and uses Gibbs sampling to generate posterior draws, yielding both shrinkage estimates for the eigenvalues and approximations to the oracle Bayes rules. In simulations, the resulting estimators come close to the risk of the oracle rules and have smaller risk than commonly used estimators, particularly when p/n is large. In an application to monthly returns of 49 US industry portfolios, the proposed estimators had the highest out-of-sample likelihood of all the estimators we compared, and their minimum-variance portfolios had variance comparable to that of estimators designed specifically for portfolio selection.

items.title: Tuning the false discovery rate in the closed eBH procedure
items.summary: The closed eBH procedure controls the false discovery rate under arbitrary dependence between the input e-values. It takes the target false discovery rate $α$ as its input and outputs a rejection set $R$, the usual goal being to maximize its size $\left|R\right|$. This note discusses a modification of the closed eBH procedure that allows choosing the target false discovery rate post hoc: the rejection set and its level $α$ can be chosen after seeing the data, and the expected ratio of the false discovery proportion to $α$ is at most 1. We adapt Vovk and Wang's (2023) algorithm for computing discovery e-matrices to computing, in quadratic time, the frontier of achievable combinations $(\left|R\right|,α)$ of the size of a rejection set $R$ and its level $α$. The frontier allows us to compute an optimal rejection set in view of a given utility function $F$, $F(\left|R\right|,α)\to\max$, striking a balance between the goals of reducing $α$ and increasing $\left|R\right|$.

items.title: On the Convergence of Multicalibration Gradient Boosting
items.summary: Multicalibration gradient boosting has recently emerged as a scalable method that empirically produces approximately multicalibrated predictors and has been deployed at web scale. Despite this empirical success, its convergence properties are not well understood. In this paper, we provide computational guarantees for multicalibration gradient boosting algorithms. We show that the magnitude of successive prediction updates decays at $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ (in the minimum over $T$ rounds), which implies the same convergence rate bound for the empirical multicalibration error over rounds. For the squared-error loss, this rate improves to linear convergence under additional smoothness assumptions on the weak learners, and convergence extends to relaxed and adaptive rescaling variants. Combining the empirical bound with uniform convergence arguments, we also bound the population multicalibration error for the log-loss under additional conditions on the weak learners, which yields a prescription for the number of rounds as a function of the sample size. Experiments on real-world datasets support our theory, clarify the regimes in which the method achieves fast convergence, and show that early stopping is needed on held-out data.

items.title: A Wasserstein Trust-Region Method for Smooth Potential-Interaction Energies
items.summary: Finding low-energy particle configurations and approximating probability distributions both lead to minimizing potential-interaction energies in Wasserstein space. Second-order information can speed up minimizing these possibly nonconvex energies, but a quadratic model is accurate only near the current measure. We introduce a Wasserstein trust-region (WTR) method for smooth, possibly nonconvex energies of this type. Each iteration transports the current measure $ρ$ along a displacement field $s$, producing $(\mathrm{Id}+s)_\#ρ$. The field approximately minimizes a quadratic model built from the second variation of the energy, subject to $\|s\|_{L^2(ρ)}\leΔ$, using a truncated conjugate-gradient method. The ratio of actual to predicted decrease determines step acceptance and updates the trust-region radius. Under a lower energy bound and globally bounded Hessians of the potential and interaction kernel, we prove that the objective is nonincreasing, the Wasserstein-gradient norms converge to zero, and an $\varepsilon$-stationary iterate is reached within $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ iterations, rejected ones included. If the potential is quadratically coercive, every weak accumulation point is stationary. For empirical measures, WTR is an ordinary trust-region method in the particle positions, and its complexity bound does not depend on the number of particles provided the initial energy exceeds its infimum by a bounded amount. For $2048$ and $4096$ particles with Gaussian pair repulsion in a two-dimensional harmonic trap, WTR reaches the gradient tolerance $2\times10^{-4}$ a median $1.40$ times faster than L-BFGS. For equal-weight integration rules on two non-Gaussian targets, WTR reaches an integration error of $10^{-4}$ about $1.8$ times faster than L-BFGS and $1.3$ times faster than a Krylov trust-region solver.

items.title: Robust Forest-based Estimation of Heterogeneous Treatment Effect Under High-dimensional Confounding
items.summary: Understanding how patients with Alzheimer's disease respond differently to treatment is important for individualized therapeutic assessment. Using observational data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), we investigate how the association between donepezil dosage and 12-month cognitive performance varies across diagnostic stages and hippocampal volumes. This analysis presents several statistical challenges, including potentially nonlinear treatment effect heterogeneity, high-dimensional confounding, and heavy-tailed outcomes with extreme observations. To address these challenges, we develop an Orthogonal Huber Random Forest (OHRF) framework that combines Huber-based robust estimation, Neyman orthogonality, and forest-based adaptive weighting. The proposed method accommodates complex treatment effect heterogeneity while reducing sensitivity to nuisance estimation errors and extreme outcomes. We establish its consistency, asymptotic normality, and finite-sample error bounds. Simulation studies demonstrate favorable estimation accuracy and robustness across a range of error distributions, particularly under heavy-tailed noise and outlier contamination. In the ADNI application, OHRF produces generally narrower pointwise confidence intervals than the conventional Orthogonal Random Forest (ORF) while revealing distinct patterns of treatment effect heterogeneity across diagnostic groups and hippocampal volumes. These findings illustrate the potential of robust, data-adaptive methods for studying heterogeneous treatment responses in complex observational biomedical data.

items.title: Stein Guidance without Gradients: Discretization Uniform Diffusion Inference Time Scaling beyond Particle SMC
items.summary: Reward-guided diffusion requires effective steering and correction of the bias introduced by approximate value functions. A Brownian example shows that SMC with full multinomial resampling at every step can require particle counts to grow linearly with guidance depth to maintain accuracy. We propose Stein Guidance, which combines derivative-free guidance with whole-path independence Metropolis-Hastings correction. Value-weighted selection from centered Gaussian candidates approximates gradient guidance in expectation, using as few as two queries per step. Centering stabilizes the local normalizer estimates, and the same queries yield an explicit path weight for correction. Under uniform value and spatial regularity bounds, we prove superpolynomial decay of finite-grid total variation error in the number of MH updates, with constants that do not grow with guidance depth. The error prefactor tends to zero as the value functions approach exact Doob values and the time grid is refined.

items.title: Statistical Inference with Ill-Conditioned Random Weight Neural Network Sieves
items.summary: Random weight neural networks (RWNNs) are shallow networks whose hidden-layer parameters are randomly generated and then kept fixed, while only the output coefficients are estimated. Conditional on the sampled parameters, RWNN regression is a linear sieve problem with random approximation space. We show that such random sieves cannot remain uniformly well-conditioned as their dimension grows. For parametrized feature families satisfying polynomial covering and Lipschitz conditions, the eigenvalues of the population covariance matrix are proven to have polynomial upper bounds determined by the covering geometry of the parameter space, leading to a vanishing smallest eigenvalue. We develop approximation, estimation, and inference theory that explicitly treats the ill-conditioning. Under a $β$-Hölder source condition, we obtain both faster-than-Monte-Carlo $L^2$ approximation rates and new $L^\infty$ approximation bounds based on stratified sampling. We then derive improved consistency guarantees for ridge-regularized least squares driven by ridge effective dimension, spectral, and leverage-based stability conditions. For inference, we establish asymptotic linearity and Gaussian limits for linear functional directions while allowing the smallest eigenvalue of the population covariance matrix to vanish. Nondegeneracy is directional: we characterize it with a ridge-normalized Rayleigh quotient and extend it to smooth functionals via Riesz representation. Consistency of ridge-adjusted variance estimators is proved, yielding feasible studentized inference. Numerical experiments illustrate the deterioration of random-feature conditioning and the finite-sample behavior of the resulting estimation and inference procedures.

items.title: KernelMix: Bayesian kernel machine regression in Python
items.summary: Exposures measured together can have nonlinear associations with an outcome, and the association with one exposure may depend on another. Bayesian kernel machine regression represents these patterns through a flexible exposure-response function. We implement this approach in KernelMix, a Python package. To handle different outcome types, KernelMix combines the exposure function with continuous, binary, count and survival models, including selected extensions for clustered observations and censored event times. For fitted models, it returns posterior summaries, uncertainty intervals, joint predictions and sampling diagnostics. Fitting and prediction use NumPy and SciPy without requiring R. To assess the implementation, we compare selected Gaussian and probit posterior summaries and conditional calculations with installed R bkmr 0.2.2 and check additional model components against independent mathematical calculations. A daily ozone analysis illustrates how these components form an analysis workflow.

items.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Sample Complexity of Natural Policy Gradient with a Matching Information-Theoretic Lower Bound
items.summary: A fundamental question in reinforcement learning is how many sampled transitions are needed to learn a near-optimal policy, and whether direct policy optimization can attain this statistical limit. To answer this question, we consider natural policy gradient (NPG), a widely used policy optimization method. We study tabular finite-horizon Markov decision processes (MDPs) with known rewards and unknown horizon-dependent transition kernels, accessed through a generative model. Our sample-based NPG algorithms update the policy by backward sweeps and do not estimate transition probabilities. Under three different batch-size and step size schedules, we establish last-iterate guarantees with sample complexity $\widetilde O(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$, where $S$, $A$, and $H$ denote the number of states, the number of actions, and the horizon length, respectively. In this setting, horizon-dependent transition kernels contribute a factor of $H$ to our transition-query bound. Our information-theoretic lower bound of $Ω(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$ shows that the resulting $H^4$ dependence is unavoidable in the worst case, even for agents that select their queries adaptively. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first last-iterate guarantees for NPG whose sample complexity matches an information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Consequently, our results demonstrate that direct policy-space optimization through NPG can achieve the fundamental statistical limits of reinforcement learning while guaranteeing the performance of the final policy. Furthermore, for known kernels, we prove that exact NPG with a constant step size $η=1/H$ requires $Ω(H^2/\varepsilon)$ iterations in the worst case, matching the known upper bound for that step size.

items.title: Neural Schrödinger Bridge via Yasue Action with Applications to Generative Modeling
items.summary: We propose a novel neural solver for inferring the continuous state evolution of the Schrödinger bridge problem. The proposed solver builds on a saddle point formulation involving the Yasue action functional. This allows us to realize the continuous state evolution by learning the optimal velocity for an ordinary differential equation, as opposed to learning the optimal drift for a stochastic differential equation. The proposed solver only uses the source and the target samples, and not the source and target distributions per se, which makes it particularly suitable for high dimensional applications arising in generative modeling. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed solver using several numerical experiments in low and high dimensions, using both real and synthetic datasets.

items.title: Econometric vs. Causal structure learning for time-series data: Implications for policy interventions using COVID-19 data
items.summary: This study compares regression-based and causal structure-learning approaches to recovering temporal dependencies in UK COVID-19 data and assesses their suitability for policy analysis. We evaluate four econometric methods and eleven structure-learning algorithms using a common lag-expanded dataset that permits edges only from past to current variables. The dataset comprises 866 daily observations and 45 variables, represented by 55 numeric series after categorical encoding. Maximum lags of 1, 7, 14, 17 and 21 days are examined; all four econometric methods and ten structure-learning algorithms successfully return structures at every lag specification. We compare graph structure, complexity, fit and temporal-edge stability across lag specifications. The resulting graphs vary substantially in density, complexity, fit and stability. Agreement with the knowledge graph is limited, while low structural Hamming distance sometimes reflects sparsity rather than recovery of known relationships. Edge recurrence also varies markedly by method, revealing sensitivity to the allowed history window. Diagnostics for VAR models using all lagged predictors indicate residual dependence, non-normality and instability; estimation becomes infeasible at longer lag orders. Policy evaluation raises further concerns: few mobility-to-infection links emerge, few meet the empirical coverage criterion, and none do so in longer-lag analyses. Common temporal constraints therefore do not resolve methodological disagreement. Learnt dependency structures should not be treated as policy-ready causal models without stronger identification assumptions, robustness checks and sufficient empirical support for the interventions assessed.

items.title: The Curved Exponential Family of Cylindrical Distributions: m-Projection, Curvature and a Test of the von Mises-Fisher Component
items.summary: Cylindrical data pair a vector in R^d with a direction in S^(m-1). We study a family in which the direction is von Mises-Fisher and, given the direction, the vector is Gaussian with mean affine in it; this generalizes the Mardia-Sutton model. The family is a curved exponential family inside a regular family with Fisher-Bingham directions. We state necessary and sufficient conditions for the maximum-likelihood estimator to exist and be unique. The estimator is explicit except for one scalar root and is the m-projection (Kullback-Leibler projection) of the moment-matching member. Every moment it does not match is a function of one residual, the gap between the sample and fitted second moments of the direction. The squared length of this gap in the Fisher metric is the classical score test of von Mises-Fisher against Fisher-Bingham directions, due to Cox on the circle and extended by Mardia, Holmes and Kent. Specific here are this reading and the exact invariance of its law to the regression part. The exponential curvature lies only in the directions of the regression matrix. In closed form, the information lost on this matrix against the expected information is m-1 observations for uniform directions and (m+1)^2/(m-1) in the limit of high concentration; conditioning on the directions recovers it. Finite mixtures are identifiable. On buoy records the test rejects von Mises-Fisher directions, and generalized von Mises directions raise the held-out log-density by 0.45 nats per observation with one component.

items.title: Tight Mistake-Abstention Tradeoffs for Sequential Prediction under Adversarial Injections
items.summary: We study the sequential prediction problem introduced by Goel et al. (2023), where an adversary can inject arbitrarily many corrupted instances in an i.i.d. stream from a clean distribution $μ$, while the learner is allowed to abstain from making a prediction at no cost if the current instance was indeed injected. When $μ$ is unknown, Yu and Blanchard (2026) show a polynomial tradeoff between mistakes and false abstentions for classes with finite VC dimension and oblivious adversaries, but still leave open a significant gap between upper and lower bounds in their tradeoff landscape. In this paper, we propose the weighted shattering potential, and based on variants of this potential, provide gap-closing algorithms that essentially characterize the tradeoffs under various settings of interest: When $μ$ is known, our algorithm improves over Goel et al. (2023) and achieves their conjectured $O(d\log T)$ mistake bound; When $μ$ is unknown, for oblivious adversary, our guarantees are tight both in $T$ and in terms of the VC dimension $d$, which completely characterizes the abstention-mistake tradeoff in this setting and gives an $O(\sqrt{dT})$ balanced rate. For adaptive adversary, our results are tight up to $\operatorname{poly}(dD\log T)$ factors for structured classes with finite so-called reduction dimension $D$. Our guarantees also extend to censored feedback, where the label is hidden after an abstention.

items.title: Complex band-limited maximum likelihood: estimating the wave behind detected quanta
items.summary: Detected photons and electrons land at positions drawn from $|ψ|^2$, yet it is $ψ$, phase included, that a wave equation propagates, and the state that produced the particles is often known only in part. A density estimator can recover $|ψ|^2$ directly from the positions, without any wave equation, but it discards the phase, and with it the state. We introduce complex band-limited maximum likelihood (complex BLML), which estimates $ψ$ itself by maximising the likelihood of the detected positions over exactly the intensities the physics allows: squared moduli of complex functions whose spectrum lies in a given set, such as a band, the shape of the aperture, or several modes for a partially coherent source. A single eigenvalue can certify a global maximum. On simulated two-slit far fields we measure what each prior is worth: a band reaches a given accuracy with seven times fewer photons than a kernel density estimate and already gives the fringe contrast and the relative phase, and the shape of the aperture adds the slit geometry. Some quantities need a prior at any number of photons: for slits of one profile the intensity fixes only the contrast $2ρV/(1+ρ^2)$, and on a line two different apertures can produce the same particles. Cutting a pattern to a few fringes, as published records are, removes the slit width. On four public single-particle double-slit records it predicts held-out particles best among the methods we tested, kernel estimators and two-slit optical models included, and it recovers the fringe contrast without a model of the optics. On fluorescent beads it finds the resolution limit of the microscope, $2\mathrm{NA}/λ$, from the photons alone.

items.title: When and Where to Transfer: Learning Transferable Historical Contexts for Short-History Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
items.summary: Related sources can improve multivariate time series forecasting when the target history is short, but their usefulness varies across source groups and historical periods. A key challenge is to identify informative historical contexts from the sources. This paper proposes Hierarchical Context Transfer (HiCT), a framework that adaptively weights source groups and their historical contexts to determine both \emph{where} and \emph{when} to transfer. A shared context encoder and cross-attention are used to learn weights over source groups and historical contexts. These weights guide regularized transfer estimation, followed by an optional target-specific correction. This paper establishes a target excess-risk bound for the context-weighted transfer estimator. Experiments demonstrate competitive predictive performance across four multivariate forecasting datasets and a favorable accuracy--runtime trade-off against the evaluated baselines. Source-corruption ablations illustrate the roles of group-level and within-group weighting in adapting to unreliable source histories.

items.title: LEAF: Calibrated and Robust Wavelet Estimation of the Hurst Exponent
items.summary: Wavelet logscale regression for the Hurst exponent H of fractional Brownian motion (fBm) is sensitive to outliers and biased in finite samples. We introduce the Log-Energy with Adaptive Floor (LEAF) ordinate, which averages the logarithms of squared wavelet coefficients after adding a floor proportional to a pilot estimate of the level variance. If standardized coefficients share a common law across levels, a floor proportional to the true level variance preserves the population slope, and a consistent pilot preserves it asymptotically. We derive the asymptotic variance and influence function, and identify the variance-minimizing floor for median-pilot LEAF, whose influence grows only logarithmically. With outliers of ten increment standard deviations in up to 1% of observations, median-pilot LEAF reduces root mean squared error by a factor of 1.8 to 2.6 relative to calibrated log-energy. At H = 0.5 with 1% outliers, the error falls from 0.139 to 0.059. For small to moderate H, the main source of bias is the departure of expected wavelet energies from the ideal power law at fine scales. We estimate H from an estimating equation calibrated by simulation under fBm. Calibrating the mean logscale diagram alone delivers nearly all of the gain: it nearly eliminates bias in matched simulations and improves on the Abry--Veitch estimator most at small H. Simulations also show how scale-dependent tails can erode the gains of a robust pilot and how misspecification can undermine calibration.

items.title: Shortest Path Lengths in Poisson Line Cox Processes: Approximations and Applications
items.summary: We study street-constrained ($\ell_1$) shortest paths in a Poisson line Cox process (PLCP), where Poisson points of linear intensity $μ$ lie on the lines of an underlying Poisson line process (PLP) of density $λ$. Under a one-turn restriction, we derive closed-form expressions for the distribution of the nearest-neighbor path length from (i) the typical PLCP point and (ii) the typical PLP intersection, by explicitly evaluating the relevant void probabilities via a geometric decomposition of the feasible path-length set. For the intersection case, we further provide analytically tractable upper and lower bounds that capture the impact of $λ$ and $μ$. Allowing two turns from the typical point, we obtain a computable upper bound using a feasible-set shrinking argument and identify regimes in which it is tight. We also delineate parameter ranges where a one-turn route from a typical intersection can outperform a two-turn route from a typical point. Finally, we discuss how the results enable statistical performance characterization of ride-hailing services in terms of service guarantee, trip time, and consequently, derive dimensioning insights. We also illustrate qualitatively, how the results can be employed to study vehicle-to-vehicle communication broadcast messages near intersections.

items.title: Convex Mixed-Integer Programming for Causal Additive Models with Optimization and Statistical Guarantees
items.summary: We study the problem of learning a directed acyclic graph from data generated by an additive, nonlinear structural equation model with Gaussian noise. We represent each nonlinear function through a basis expansion and derive a maximum likelihood estimator with group l0 regularization on the graph edges and l2 regularization on their strengths, with extensions to accommodate interaction effects. A key computational contribution is a scalable mixed-integer formulation that projects out the continuous model parameters, yields a convex objective in the remaining variables, and enables a tailored cutting-plane algorithm that is guaranteed to return a solution with a prespecified optimality gap. Our formulation can also incorporate background knowledge, including known edge presence or absence and partial ordering constraints. We establish consistency for graph recovery when the number of variables grows with the sample size. By linking optimization guarantees to statistical error bounds, we further derive an early stopping criterion in the cutting-plane algorithm that preserves consistency. Compared with existing approaches that assume equal error variances, restrict attention to linear structural equation models, or rely on heuristics, our method provides both optimization and statistical guarantees. Extensive simulations and two real-data analyses show markedly improved graph recovery.

items.title: When AI Performance Is Not Enough: Statistical Guardrails for Clinical Development
items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are reshaping the operational and inferential landscape of clinical development, yet their adoption frequently outpaces the statistical scrutiny these methods demand. This commentary offers first-principles perspectives across four application domains: anomaly detection in clinical trial data, real-time monitoring and adaptive trial designs, biomarker-based enrichment, and virtual and digital twins. For each domain, we articulate the underlying inferential problem, the contribution of AI and ML relative to established statistical methods, and the risks that statisticians, data scientists, and clinical developers must actively manage. Across these domains, a unifying theme emerges: AI and ML methods may succeed locally while failing to satisfy the broader statistical assumptions required for valid clinical and regulatory decisions. These risks include false-positive signals, compromised Type I error control in adaptive designs, conflation of prognostic with predictive biomarkers, and causal claims not supported by data and assumptions. We argue that a clearly defined context of use, relevant statistical assumptions, and consequences of the intended decision should guide the evaluation. For treatment-effect questions, the ICH E9(R1) estimand framework provides a useful organizing principle. Responsible use of AI in clinical development requires not restraint, but rigor: the inferential discipline necessary to make these technologies reproducible, interpretable, and defensible in the service of patients.

items.title: A nudge among nudges: when the field pushes back
items.summary: Behavioural interventions are designed and tested as if the setting they enter stays put. But other actors push the same people, watch the behaviour and respond when it moves. The paper asks what becomes of a nudge in such a field. In an agent-based model, people act when their inclination and the pushes they feel cross a threshold, nudges compete for limited attention, and other actors steer the behaviour's rate towards their own goals without seeing the nudge. Calibrated to published effect sizes, it reproduces four documented regularities, one of them by calibration. The same nudge meets five fates, set by who else acts: attenuated, transient, null, reversed, or a blind site, where a sound field experiment reports nearly the full effect while its site gains little. Where the field reacts, a pilot's own comparison does not forecast the rollout: it cannot see the response the pilot provokes, and a small pilot does not exhaust the competitor as the rollout does. The fate follows from a few quantities, with nothing fitted after the calibration; the derivation matched the simulation on eight of ten maps of settings. Across 49,152 random settings, each with a competitor, the expected effect was the exception; what shifted the fate most depended on how attention is shared: the nudge's strength when the strongest nudge is heard first, the number of competing nudges when it is split. Whether a real field reacts can be read from marks a trial could record, such as drift among the untreated.

items.title: A hybrid Graph-based Machine Learning Model for predicting Delivery Times in Supply Chain Logistics
items.summary: Global supply chains are increasingly vulnerable to disruptions arising from external events, such as natural disasters and geopolitical crises, and from internal operational inefficiencies, including supplier delays and bottlenecks in order shipping. This work, conducted within the Horizon Europe project M4ESTRO, introduces a hybrid modelling approach combining graph theory and machine learning to represent supply chain logistics operations, with a focus on predicting delays in inbound flows between industrial suppliers and manufacturing entities. The various stages of order fulfilment are modelled through a formal mathematical framework, by defining disruption indicators computed from both historical and real-time data drawn from heterogeneous sources, including traffic and weather conditions and supplier dispatch readiness. Building on a graph-based representation of the supply chain, stochastic methods based on Markov chains are applied to estimate delivery times, detect schedule deviations, quantify prediction uncertainty, and produce interpretable metrics to support operational decision-making. Within the M4ESTRO project, the proposed framework was applied to build a web application for real-time tracking of inbound logistics, and was validated in a use case with an industrial project partner. The web application successfully enabled early detection of logistics disruptions along the supply chain and provided stakeholders with the visibility needed to act before delays propagated. The underlying model proved effective as the basis of a resilient, data-driven logistics tracking system, aligned with the digital transformation objectives of industry and with Manufacturing-as-a-Service paradigms.

items.title: Guidance-Induced Activation of Score Estimation Errors in Diffusion Models
items.summary: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) combines conditional and unconditional score estimates to steer diffusion sampling. The weighted-solenoidal component of each score error has no instantaneous effect on the evolution of its corresponding reference density. Because the guided density in CFG generally differs from both reference densities, the combination of these solenoidal components can affect the evolution of the guided marginals. We call this mechanism guidance-induced error activation. Using a weighted Helmholtz-Hodge decomposition, we identify the activated error field, quantify its magnitude, and characterize when it vanishes. At fixed noise time, the activated error field varies continuously with guidance strength. Its weak first-order variation has two terms, one from reweighting the errors and one from the change in the guided density. For finite score errors, ODE characteristics and an SDE Feynman-Kac formula connect error-activation to the generated densities. For a class of finite Gaussian mixtures, error-activation can account for most of the KL divergence between the generated distributions by learned-score and exact-score CFG ODE samplers under strong guidance. Ideal score filtering removes the weighted-solenoidal errors and eliminates error-activation. Controlled experiments with Gaussian and Gamma mixtures illustrate how activation affects the generated densities. Qualitative CIFAR-10 comparisons suggest that filtering can help preserve object structure under strong guidance.

items.title: A complete characterization of sequential testability and change detectability in i.i.d. models
items.summary: We give qualitative and quantitative necessary and sufficient conditions for sequential testing and change detection in an i.i.d. composite problem. A level-\(α\) test with power one against every alternative exists if and only if the alternatives are separated from the null by a countable family of finite-block events. Equivalent conditions use randomized tests, bounded scores, e-processes, reduced-filtration test supermartingales, and a countable cover with positive finite-block weak-$*$ convex-hull separation. The construction gives pointwise expected sample size \(O_Q(\log(1/α))\). Quantitatively, one e-process attains the intrinsic pointwise growth rate \(Γ(Q)\) at every alternative if and only if a countable family of bounded block bets recovers these rates. The same condition characterizes simultaneous attainment of the sharp expected-sample-size coefficient \(1/Γ(Q)\); arbitrary attainable lower rate profiles admit an analogous characterization. Total-variation separability of the alternatives suffices for recovery. Weak lower semicontinuity of the KL projection, in particular weak compactness of the null, also identifies \(Γ(Q)\) with \(\inf_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathrm{KL}(Q\|P)\). The qualitative and quantitative conditions also characterize change detectability under fixed-time false-alarm bounds \(\Prob_{P^\infty}(T_γ\le n)\le n/γ\), together with ordinary ARL control. Whenever countable rate recovery holds, for any \(η>0\) one calibrated e-detector has robust Lorden delay asymptotic to \((\logγ)/Γ(Q)\) at finite positive rates, while satisfying the stronger optional-horizon inequality and placing every null ARL in \([γ,(1+η)γ+1]\). Examples exhibit a strict cost of simultaneous optimality and show that ordinary ARL alone supports neither characterization, even with finite, tightly calibrated null means.

items.title: A Bayesian Mechanistic Model of Spatiotemporal Dynamics in Invasive Tree Species
items.summary: Modeling the spatiotemporal dynamics of invasive species requires frameworks that represent spread and growth mechanisms explicitly while accommodating the distributional features of ecological data. We propose a Bayesian mechanistic framework for invasive tree cover that combines an ecological diffusion--logistic growth partial differential equation (PDE) with a zero-inflated binomial observation model. The diffusion and growth coefficients are modeled as functions of environmental covariates, enabling direct inference on the ecological processes driving encroachment, and the zero-inflation component separates structural absence from low observed cover. To enable scalable Bayesian inference on satellite-resolution grids, we derive a homogenized equation for ecological diffusion with spatially varying diffusion and growth coefficients, which reduces computation while preserving large-scale spatial structure. Applied to satellite-derived tree cover in a subregion of the Nebraska Sandhills, where eastern redcedar is encroaching on grassland, the model indicates that elevation is strongly associated with where tree cover accumulates but only weakly with its local growth rate, whereas distance to the nearest stream is associated with both. Compared with a generalized additive model, a spatial hierarchical model fitted via INLA, and a regression tree, the proposed method directly estimates these processes as interpretable functions of environmental covariates and gives the best-calibrated predictive uncertainty.

items.title: Uncertainty quantification of fatigue initiation life for powder bed fusion metal additive manufacturing
items.summary: Predicting fatigue life with quantified uncertainties is essential for the qualification of critical components produced by laser-based powder bed fusion additive manufacturing. We present a framework that propagates microstructure and defect uncertainties directly to a fatigue initiation life distribution for a specific part. In particular, microstructure and defect characterizations are obtained from electron backscatter diffraction and micro-computed tomography scan data, which in turn inform three physics-based simulations yielding the fatigue-affecting quantities: the elastic energy release rate, the surface energy along the crack path, and the fatigue indicator parameter. Accounting for the uncertainties in these quantities and the high correlations among them due to the shared underlying microstructure, we derive a closed-form probability density function for the fatigue initiation life. This provides an analytical distribution instead of conservative deterministic predictions and enables more informed decision making for the qualification and deployment of additively manufactured components. Applying the framework to 316L stainless steel parts produced by an EOS M290 laser powder bed fusion machine, we find that both grain sizes and void distributions influence the fatigue initiation life distribution. Specifically, for a fixed total void volume fraction, larger grain sizes cause a marginal reduction in fatigue initiation life, and a population of many small voids is more favorable for fatigue life than fewer, larger voids of equivalent total volume.

items.title: Targeted Learning for Externally Controlled Trials and Beyond
items.summary: This paper focuses on externally controlled trials (ECTs), which consist of a single-arm clinical trial supplemented by an external control arm (ECA). Potential data sources for the ECA can be broadly classified into three categories: (i) the control arm of a historical clinical trial, (ii) a concurrent cohort study, and (iii) external real-world data (RWD). In this paper, we consider a broad class of estimands defined through balancing weights. For a given estimand in the class, we discuss the efficient influence function (EIF) and the targeted maximum likelihood estimator (TMLE), together with practical implementation algorithms. Within the targeted learning framework, TMLE is a substitution estimator that enjoys several desirable theoretical properties and favorable finite-sample performance. Finally, the proposed framework is extended to two additional settings: (1) randomized controlled trials (RCTs) augmented with external covariate information to define a target population, and (2) indirect treatment comparisons (ITCs) that combine individual patient data (IPD) from an internal RCT with aggregate data (AgD) from an external RCT.

items.title: Neural-network-powered new-physics searches by predictive goodness of fit
items.summary: Model-independent searches for new physics test whether data agree with a Reference model with unknown nuisance parameters. Because the shape and location of a signal are not specified, these tests call for flexible learners (fitting procedures such as neural networks), and a likelihood ratio maximized over a neural network falls outside the standard asymptotic theory, making the calibration a major challenge. We propose a predictive alternative: the departure from the Reference is fitted on part of the data and its likelihood gain over the fitted Reference is evaluated on the rest, cross-fitted over several folds to preserve sample efficiency. The nuisance estimation error is propagated into the variance of the test statistic to first order, in the spirit of Neyman's C(alpha) test, so that the test need not be recalibrated at each nuisance value. The randomness in the fitted departure is treated by a central limit theorem for cross-validated statistics under algorithmic stability, plus a variance correction when stability is not achieved. The calibration is analytic, and no pseudo-experiments are needed. On established one-dimensional and five-dimensional (dilepton) benchmarks, the false-positive rate always stays within Monte Carlo error of nominal across different nuisances and the learners' tuning. The test's power relative to existing learned tests is mixed: higher for some signals and lower for others, depending on how well the fitted departure captures the signal.

items.title: Geometric ergodicity of Gibbs samplers for linear mixed models with several heavy-tailed random-effect components and unknown tail parameters
items.summary: Linear mixed models with heavy-tailed random effects are widely used for robust Bayesian analysis of longitudinal data. We study the three-block Gibbs sampler for such models when the random effects are split into several components, such as random intercepts and slopes, each with its own scale and its own scale mixture of normals, when the tail parameters have priors on finite grids and are drawn jointly with the latent weights, and when the random-effects design is rank deficient, as when some subjects contribute a single observation. We give sufficient conditions for geometric ergodicity that attribute the rank deficiency to the components that cause it, and show that, under conditions on the gamma priors on the precision parameters, they hold for Student-t and slash random effects with individual weights, any grid of tail parameters and any design. The result extends to random-effect vectors whose coordinates share a weight, for subject-specific designs with known shape matrices. It justifies Monte Carlo standard errors for regression coefficients, log-scales and posterior probabilities of the tail parameters. Simulations show that the scale and the tail parameter can mix much more slowly than the regression coefficients, and an analysis of beta-HCG data illustrates the methods.

items.title: On numerical issues of divergences between nearly equal distributions
items.summary: Barron et al. (2026) recently identified numerical issues in the softmax and soft cross-entropy loss. We show that similar issues are present in standard divergence operations between categorical distributions. This includes the forward and reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence and generalized Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD), as well as Monte Carlo KL estimates and entropy. When the distributions are nearly equal, rounding and cancellation issues affect the forward and gradient computations. These issues can affect settings using divergences in optimization objectives, such as knowledge distillation, reinforcement learning, and proximal methods. We propose numerically stable reformulations and provide example implementations for each setting, validated by property-based tests.

items.title: Kinetic versus refill-zone uncertainty in predicted pr--burning of methane-oxygen rotating detonation rocket engines
items.summary: Rotating detonation rocket engines can lose performance when fresh propellant mixes with hot recirculated combustion products and ignites before the detonation wave arrives. Predicting this pre-burning requires fuel ignition chemistry at high pressure and in product-diluted mixtures, conditions most chemical kinetic mechanisms used in engine simulations were not developed for. With methane as our base fuel, we quantify how strongly predicted pre-burning depends on the choice of mechanism, test the mechanisms against published high-pressure ignition data, and use Bayesian methods to calibrate the most influential uncertain reaction and to assess which measurements would best improve the predictions. As the refill zone is represented by an idealized zero-dimensional model, our results should be viewed as relative comparisons rather than direct engine predictions. Five existing chemical kinetics mechanisms for methane combustion predict refill-zone ignition delays that differ by up to a factor of twenty. Mechanisms without methylperoxy chemistry, including two commonly used in engine simulations, do not reproduce the laboratory data below about 1150 K. Calibrating the CH${_3}$ + HO${_2}$ reaction against these data, while allowing for systematic differences between datasets, increases the relative importance of its chain-terminating channel, consistent with a direct rate measurement. With the data-consistent mechanisms, the remaining kinetic uncertainty in the predicted pre-burnt fraction is, in most cases, several times smaller than the uncertainty arising from the state of the refill zone: the temperature and composition of the recirculated products and the way fresh and burnt gases mix. Improved pre-burning predictions are therefore expected to depend mainly on accurately characterizing the refill zone.

items.title: Data-Dependent Probability Estimation via Sample Amplification
items.summary: Can we estimate the probability of an event chosen after seeing the data, without using any fresh samples? Its empirical probability can be arbitrarily misleading, while learning the entire distribution to constant accuracy requires $Θ(d)$ samples on a domain of size $d$. We show that $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d})$ samples suffice for constant mean squared error, provided the rule choosing the event is known. More generally, our estimator handles arbitrary $[0,1]$-valued queries and runs in polynomial time given evaluation access to the rule. This sample complexity matches the known lower bound up to logarithmic factors and resolves the open question posed by Feldman, Kale, Raman, Talwar, and Tewari (arXiv:2610.41244). Our estimation framework relies on a new combination of sample amplification (arXiv:1904.12053 and arXiv:2201.04315) with distribution learning via online optimization. Our estimator achieves mean squared error $O(d^{3/4}/n)$ when $d\leq n$ and $\widetilde{O}(d^{1/4}/\sqrt{n})$ when $d>n$. We complement this with a lower bound of $Ω(\min\{1,\sqrt{d}/n\})$ on the mean squared error. Using our framework, we also design an efficient estimator for data-dependent queries on Gaussian distributions with unknown mean and identity covariance. Finally, we show that a smoothed variant of the problem is much (exponentially) easier. For discrete distributions, if the sample size is chosen uniformly from $\{n,\ldots,2n-1\}$, then $n=O(\log d)$ suffices for constant mean squared error.

items.title: Boolean threshold functions, neuron capacity, and memory retrieval
items.summary: How much information can a single neuron remember? How many memories can neural networks retrieve without creating false memories? These questions are related to a basic question: how many Boolean threshold functions $f(x)=\operatorname{sgn}(a_0+\langle a,x\rangle)$, $x\in\{-1,1\}^n$, are there? In this paper, we show that the number $T_n$ of distinct Boolean threshold functions is \[ T_n=2\binom{2^n-1}{n}\bigl(1+O(n^{-99})\bigr). \] Equivalently, the capacity of a single threshold neuron is $n^2-\log_2(n!)+1+O(n^{-99})$ bits, improving the $O(n)$ error term in the result of Kahn--Komlós--Szemerédi to $O(n^{-99})$. To prove this, we show that, for $1\le r\le n-1$, and $v_1,\ldots,v_r$ are chosen at random from $\{-1,1\}^n$, \[ \mathbb P\!\left\{ \langle v_1,\ldots,v_r\rangle\cap\{-1,1\}^n =\{\pm v_1,\ldots,\pm v_r\} \right\} =1-O(n^{-99}). \] In the context of the Kanter--Sompolinsky Hamiltonian for memory retrieval, this identifies $r=n-1$ as a sharp threshold, at which, for almost every collection of $r$ memories, the only ground states are these memories and their negatives, confirming a weaker form of the Kalai--Linial--Odlyzko conjecture. It also settles a recent open problem posed by M. Anthony on the specification number of Boolean threshold functions. In addition, we show that, for every $1\le r\le n-1$, \[ \mathbb P\{v_1,\ldots,v_r\text{ are linearly dependent}\} =2\binom r2\,2^{-n}+O\!\left(2^{-n}e^{-cn}\right), \] confirming a conjecture of Kahn--Komlós--Szemerédi.

items.title: Amortized Inference for Correlated Discrete Choice Models via Equivariant Neural Networks
items.summary: Discrete choice models are fundamental tools in management science, economics, and marketing. Logit models dominate applied work because they yield closed-form choice probabilities, but IID Gumbel errors impose restrictive substitution patterns. We propose an amortized inference approach based on a neural network emulator that approximates choice probabilities under general, potentially correlated, error distributions. We develop a specialized neural network architecture respecting the invariance properties of discrete choice models and provide group-theoretic foundations for universal approximation from a minimal set of invariant features. Using Sobolev training, the emulator learns choice probabilities and their derivatives, enabling rapid likelihood and gradient evaluation. We show that emulator-based maximum likelihood estimators are consistent and asymptotically normal under mild approximation conditions. Simulations show substantial gains over the GHK simulator in accuracy and speed. Using NielsenIQ data on household laundry-detergent purchases, we estimate correlated-probit and correlated-Gumbel models with rich household-level random effects. The IID period-error restriction---and hence the conditional-IIA restriction underlying conventional mixed logit---is strongly rejected. The Bayesian information criterion (BIC) selects a correlated-Gumbel model with a three-factor period-error covariance structure. We find that allowing correlated period errors materially changes predicted product substitution patterns.

items.title: Statistical inference under response-adaptive experimental designs: a systematic review
items.summary: Response-adaptive designs, including bandit-based approaches, update treatment allocation using accrued outcomes. In this paper, we systematically reviewed how studies in health and biostatistics conducted and evaluated inference under these designs. We searched six databases for studies published from January 2010 through October 2025. Of 774 records identified, 36 studies met the inclusion criteria. We summarized them using study-level counts and structured narrative comparisons, with reporting guided by PRISMA 2020. Most studies focused on methods or designs. Evidence supporting inference came mainly from theory and simulation. Among studies for which each metric was relevant, 26 of 32 numerically evaluated power, 23 of 32 type I error, eight of 35 estimator bias, and five of 12 interval coverage. These findings suggest that studies more often quantified power and type I error than estimator bias or interval coverage. Evaluations of adaptive allocation should also examine estimation and interval performance when these are relevant to the study objective.

items.title: Treatment Policy Design in the Presence of Measurement Error
items.summary: In many applications, treatments are assigned based on unit features, leading to personalized treatment policies. This often involves optimizing objective functions with counterfactual quantities such as the conditional average treatment effect (CATE). In practice, some key features may be measured with error and ignoring such errors can introduce systematic bias. We study how to design personalized treatment policies when some features are latent and only noisy measurements are available. We ask how policies can be constructed when the CATE is not identifiable, and how uncertainty from measurement error can be incorporated into policy design. We propose two frameworks for treatment policy design based on partial identification, focusing on the measurement mechanism-the conditional distribution of observed measurements given unobserved features. The first framework builds on ideas from proximal causal inference. The second adopts a modular Bayesian approach based on a reparameterized likelihood, using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and Bayesian regression models to separately perform posterior inference on the measurement mechanism and nuisance functions. Posterior quantiles are then used to construct credible intervals for the CATE that account for uncertainty in both components. Treatment policies are then derived by comparing the null value of the CATE to these bounds. The proposed methods provide a coherent way to account for measurement error and model uncertainty in personalized treatment policy design.

items.title: Beyond Gaussian Calibration: Local Inference in Decentralized SGD
items.summary: Decentralized SGD minimizes a common objective by local gradient steps and neighbor averaging. Its statistical theory mostly concerns network averages, yet clients act on their own iterates, and one-sided decisions such as alarms use one tail of the local error. We show that a client's constant-step endpoint can have nearly nominal Gaussian coverage while both tails are badly miscalibrated. An exact noise-filter representation explains why: a quantity computable from the graph and stepsize decides whether the endpoint is asymptotically Gaussian, and when the number of clients outgrows the inverse stepsize on networks with summable return probabilities, such as lazy tori of dimension at least three and expanders, a few recent noise terms at nearby clients keep a fixed share of local variance. On these tori the limit is a non-Gaussian local field plus an independent Gaussian consensus term, and no reference distribution built from finitely many noise moments, including Edgeworth and Cornish--Fisher corrections, is calibrated at all levels uniformly over noise laws. We propose a hybrid reference that resamples the influential noise terms from their empirical law and replaces the rest by a Gaussian; its non-asymptotic coverage bound allows noise laws and curvature estimated from fresh gradients or the client's trajectory, and extends to nonlinear vector objectives. In full-network simulations it restores tail balance at essentially unchanged interval length, also under rare large shocks that break Cornish--Fisher intervals; gains vanish, as predicted, when consensus dominates.

items.title: Directional Bias in Quantile SGD and Score-Inversion Inference under Dependence
items.summary: Quantile stochastic gradient descent (SGD) tracks a quantile by comparing each observation with an adaptive threshold, and closely related updates calibrate online conformal sets and drive quantile temporal-difference learning. Their inputs are serially dependent, yet existing guarantees largely assume independence. We show that dependence creates a directional bias that score autocovariances cannot detect: reversing a stationary stream leaves every score autocovariance unchanged but can change the leading bias threefold. For finite memory and decreasing stepsizes, the bias splits into lag-specific interactions between the threshold and the current observation and a curvature term; delaying the threshold removes the interactions one lag at a time while keeping every observation and the leading variance. At stepsizes near $t^{-1/2}$, as used for online inference, the bias is comparable to the standard error and makes an SGD-based interval miss mostly on one side. Testing fixed candidates instead keeps the score centered, so calibration depends only on score autocovariances. Extending local-dependence self-normalized approximations to the implemented acceptance hull, we show that inverting these tests gives a density-free, moment-free interval for the population quantile with $O(n^{-1/2})$ coverage error for a fixed sufficient lag window, a rate that is sharp for this interval, and a guarantee for data-selected windows; an exact scan takes $O(n\log n)$ time. Experiments confirm the lag-by-lag predictions and show calibration competitive with block bootstrap at lower cost.

items.title: Which Loans, Not How Many: Exactly Level-Invariant, Anytime-Valid Monitoring of Deployed Risk Models
items.summary: A refinancing wave can change the number of mortgage prepayments without changing the relationship between scores and prepayment. In a logistic model, conditioning on the monthly count removes the intercept from the likelihood of which loans prepay. Our fixed-start slope product tests a lower bound on the calibration slope. At threshold 20 its probability of ever crossing under the null is at most 5%. The restarted level sum tracks departures from intercept tolerance. A confidence sequence estimates a constant slope, and the restart-intersection rule detects changes in that slope. A continuous mixture avoids the off-grid width floor of a discrete prior. On Freddie Mac loans, fixed-slope resampling reproduces 78% of maintained-model monthly AUC variance in development and 70% in the holdout (95% intervals 57-100% and 48-100%). From fresh holdout starts, the restarted level sum crosses on both paths, and the fixed-start slope product stays below threshold on both. The restart-intersection rule signals a downward change for the frozen model in April 2018 and an upward change for the maintained model in a supplementary run in August 2019.

items.title: Bayesian Image Reconstruction and Uncertainty Quantification for Three-Photon Positronium Ratio Imaging: Toward Radiotheranostic Applications
items.summary: Three-photon annihilation imaging can estimate positronium decay ratios with pure positron emitters, including the imaging agents of radiotheranostic pairs, but quantitative reconstruction is limited by heterogeneous localization errors, selection-dependent sensitivity, and background coincidences. We develop a Bayesian reconstruction combining a three-dimensional event-response model with a Poisson likelihood and latent signal-background allocations. Photon-energy and interaction-position uncertainties enter the event covariance; a simulation-calibrated scale mixture accommodates heavy-tailed errors. Posterior sampling gives credible intervals for the three-to-two-photon enhancement ratio. We compare kernel deposition, voxel MLEM, and matched regional maximum likelihood. At 3000 selected events in full-absorption simulation, the regional Bayesian estimator had ratio RMSE 0.067, versus 0.075 for kernel-deposition region-of-interest analysis. In a transport-based four-rod simulation without background, biases averaged at most 3.2% over six independent simulations, whereas background and detector mismatch degraded it. In a measured uniform phantom, the heavy-tailed regional model gave 1.02, 0.74, 1.02 for the 2, 3, 4 mm rods (5 mm reference; nominal 1). Matched regional maximum likelihood agreed with the Bayesian estimates in every simulated setting (bias differences within 0.15 points) and on the measured data (within 0.008), so gains derive from the regional likelihood. Under Poisson Kullback-Leibler loss, Gamma posterior means dominate maximum likelihood, appreciably only at small counts; horseshoe-type and smoothing priors changed voxel images but not regional ratios, whereas shrinking ratios across regions reduced error when regions shared a ratio. Posterior intervals quantify the uncertainty that treatment decisions require; calibration and background modeling remain limiting.

items.title: Skew-Symmetric Factor Models
items.summary: The paper introduces and analyzes a factor model for (real) skew-symmetric data, which arise naturally in directed flows and in pairwise comparisons used for rankings. Working within a signal-plus-noise framework, we analyze spectral inference and establish a BBP-type phase transition in signal strength. Under Gaussian noise, we derive joint eigenvalue fluctuation limits. Above the separation threshold, the estimated signal strength is asymptotically normal whenever the population strength has multiplicity one. For a general multiplicity $k$, the joint limiting fluctuations of the corresponding sample eigenvalues above the threshold are given by the eigenvalues of a scaled $k\times k$ Gaussian unitary ensemble matrix. The skew-symmetric structure induces paired eigenspaces, and we characterize the canonical angles between the population and sample eigenspaces. Below the threshold, the corresponding largest sample eigenvalue converges to the edge of the semicircle law, with fluctuations governed by the Tracy--Widom $F_2$ distribution, in contrast to the $F_1$ law familiar from real symmetric models. The approach is illustrated through financial and demographic applications.

items.title: A CV-TMLE global test approach to improve power in rare disease clinical studies with multiple-component endpoints
items.summary: Rare disease trials face unique statistical challenges due to limited patient populations and heterogeneous clinical manifestations among patients. Multiple endpoints are often necessary to comprehensively capture treatment benefits. A global test is an approach for evaluating whether a treatment has any beneficial effect across multiple endpoints. We propose a new global test based on a weighted composite endpoint. The proposed global test employs shrinkage-based cross-validated targeted maximum likelihood estimation (CV-TMLE) to learn data-adaptive weights that maximize power while maintaining Type I error control. Shrinkage can be tailored to incorporate existing domain knowledge, such as anticipated relative effect sizes. In simulation studies designed to reflect real rare disease trial settings, the proposed procedure demonstrated improved power over standard multiplicity adjustments and classical global tests (such as the O'Brien test), while maintaining nominal Type I error, when effects are heterogeneous across endpoints. The proposed method simultaneously learns an optimal weighted composite outcome and provides an unbiased and efficient targeted maximum likelihood estimator (TMLE) for the average treatment effect (ATE) on that weighted outcome, with valid inference taking into account that the ATE is data dependent.

items.title: Vaccine sieve analysis on deep sequencing data using competing risks Cox regression with failure type subject to misclassification
items.summary: Understanding how vaccines perform against different pathogen genotypes is crucial for developing effective prevention strategies, particularly for highly genetically diverse pathogens like HIV. Sieve analysis is a statistical framework used to determine whether a vaccine selectively prevents infection by certain genotypes while allowing breakthrough of other genotypes that evade immune responses. Traditionally, these analyses are conducted with a single sequence available per individual acquiring the pathogen. However, modern sequencing technology can provide detailed characterization of intra-individual viral diversity by capturing up to hundreds of pathogen sequences per person. In this work, we introduce methodology that extends sieve analysis to account for intra-individual viral diversity. Our approach estimates vaccine efficacy against viral populations with at least a small threshold of vaccine-mismatched mutations. To account for differential resolution of information from differing sequence counts per person, we use competing risks Cox regression with modeled causes of failure and propose an empirical Bayes approach for the classification model. Simulation studies demonstrate that our approach reduces bias, provides nominal confidence interval coverage, and improves statistical power compared to conventional methods. We apply our method to the HVTN 705 Imbokodo trial, which assessed the efficacy of a heterologous vaccine regimen in preventing HIV-1 infection.

items.title: Threshold Generalized Autoregressive Moving Average Models
items.summary: Non-Gaussian time series often exhibit nonlinear dynamics and changes in dependence structures that may not be adequately captured by conventional single-regime models. To address this limitation, we introduce a class of threshold generalized autoregressive moving-average (TGARMA) models that combines observation-driven GARMA dynamics with threshold-based regime switching. The proposed framework accommodates multiple regimes, determined by a lagged endogenous or exogenous threshold variable, and allows regression coefficients, autoregressive and moving-average orders and coefficients, and, where applicable, dispersion parameters to vary across regimes. Parameters are estimated by maximum partial likelihood, while model selection is conducted using information criteria. We examine model admissibility and stability, assess model adequacy through residual diagnostics, and conduct a Monte Carlo simulation study to investigate the finite-sample performance of the estimators. The proposed methodology is illustrated using monthly counts of hospitalizations due to respiratory diseases among older adults in São Paulo, Brazil. In this application, the TGARMA model outperforms its single-regime GARMA counterpart in terms of in-sample mean squared error, highlighting the potential benefits of incorporating regime-dependent dynamics into the analysis of non-Gaussian time series.

items.title: Coresets for Density-Based Clustering via Bayesian Predictive Partition Matching
items.summary: Density-based clustering identifies groups as connected high-density regions, accommodating irregular shapes and reflecting their geometry, but this reliance on density estimation introduces uncertainty into the resulting partitions, which is often costly to quantify. To represent this uncertainty efficiently, we construct a compact representation of the data, or coreset, designed to preserve the distribution of predictive density-based partitions. We sample observations from a Dirichlet process surrogate, smooth them to estimate densities, and use the resulting level sets to partition a common reference set. Starting from a uniform subsample, we learn an affine transformation that improves agreement with full-data partitions by minimizing a tractable approximation to paired expected variation of information. Fresh, independent predictive simulations then guide the selection of the final transformation. Our analysis provides approximation and selection guarantees and establishes consistency for ideal fixed-resolution partitions under geometric conditions. Simulations and an application to mass cytometry show improved partition agreement over uniform subsampling, often matching substantially larger supports.

items.title: Probabilistic framework for infrastructure deformation anomaly warning using InSAR observations
items.summary: Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) offers a low-cost, wide-area solution for near continuous infrastructure monitoring. However, translating InSAR observations into automated anomaly warnings remains challenging because displacements are relative, affected by uncertainty, and acquired along line of sight (LOS). This paper introduces a probabilistic warning framework that accounts for these factors. LOS displacements are modelled through a Gaussian distribution. A limit state function is defined to describe the displacement exceedance, and the time-dependent probability of exceedance is evaluated. Instead of a fixed threshold, warnings are identified through abrupt increases in exceedance probability. The framework is tested using three case studies of quay walls in Amsterdam, The Netherlands, providing timely anomaly warnings and issued no warnings for the non-collapse case. Results demonstrate the potential of a probabilistic interpretation of InSAR time series for deformation anomaly warning.

items.title: Variable Importance Recovery in Tabular Foundation Models: A Simulation Study
items.summary: In machine learning, identifying which variables contribute predictive information can be as important as predictive accuracy. Tabular foundation models have matched or exceeded the predictive performance of tuned gradient boosting trees on many small- and medium-sized tabular datasets. Yet their ability to recover population-level variable importance has received little attention. We design and conduct a Monte Carlo simulation study to compare variable importance recovery across tabular foundation models and established machine learning baselines. Our framework distinguishes multiple population estimands, pairs each one with an aligned model-agnostic importance estimator, and evaluates recovery in terms of ranking, support, and relative magnitude. Our results show that tabular foundation models are generally competitive with established machine-learning baselines in recovering population variable importance, and often more accurate. We thus extend the evidence for their capabilities to a previously underexamined dimension, further strengthening their appeal.

items.title: Learning the Projection onto the Data Support: Distribution Learning that Avoids Memorization
items.summary: We introduce a framework for learning distributions supported on manifolds based on estimating the nearest-point projection onto the data support. Specifically, we define an objective functional over a class of functions whose minimizer recovers this projection. The proposed framework automatically adapts to the intrinsic dimension and allows for data supported on unions of manifolds with varying dimensions. The resulting objective can be optimized using standard neural network architectures. We present population-level results establishing recovery of the manifold projection and prove finite-sample Wasserstein generalization bounds. Furthermore, we validate the approach empirically across a range of settings. In contrast to widely used generative models such as diffusion models, whose objectives can be minimized by memorizing training samples, our formulation excludes such behavior. We also introduce a direct memorization metric to verify that the learned projection generates new samples rather than reproducing the training set.

items.title: Faster Estimates from Binned Test Scores---With Discussion of Normality, Bias, and Reliability
items.summary: Education agencies often summarize test score distributions by counting how many students scored in 3 to 5 bins. Means and standard deviations (SDs) can be estimated from bin counts using a HETOP model, which assumes that scores are normally distributed within each school or district. However, most HETOP software takes minutes to hours if the number of schools or districts is large. We present a fast HETOP algorithm that produces HETOP estimates in less than a millisecond per district. The algorithm is implemented in the fast_hetop function of the binest package for RL: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/binest/refman/binest.html#topic+fast_hetop HETOP estimates of the mean are highly reliable; estimates of the SD are not as good. Maximum likelihood estimates are generally excellent but can be biased and unreliable if scores are not normal or scores are concentrated in the top or bottom bin. Empirical Bayes shrinkage improves unreliable estimates. Standard errors are smaller if the data represents the whole population of students rather than a sample. HETOP estimates are usable for many purposes, but it would be better if education agencies reported means and SDs directly.

items.title: Conditional Independence Testing for Random Objects via Generative Models
items.summary: We propose a test of conditional independence for random objects taking values in metric spaces of negative type, allowing the conditioning variable to be either a random object or a high-dimensional vector. Our method uses multidimensional scaling and Nyström extensions to obtain finite-dimensional representations of random objects from their pairwise distances, and generative neural networks to estimate conditional distributions in the embedded space. Samples from the fitted generators are then used to construct a doubly robust test statistic. Our main theoretical contribution is to quantify how errors from estimating and truncating the embeddings, together with errors in learning the conditional distributions, affect inference. We establish conditions under which these errors are asymptotically negligible, even when the embedding dimensions grow with the sample size. In particular, we derive explicit convergence rates when the conditional distributions admit generators with smooth, low-dimensional compositional structure. We establish asymptotic validity of the bootstrap test, consistency against fixed alternatives, and nontrivial power against local alternatives. Simulations with distribution-valued data demonstrate its competitive finite-sample performance.

items.title: Optimal Linear Regression Without a Variance
items.summary: We study high-probability linear regression in the infinite variance regime, wherecthe regression noise has only a finite conditional $α$-moment $ν$ for some unknown $α\in(1,2)$, and the covariates may only have finite moments up to a given order (e.g., 4th moment). We give a black-box reduction that converts finite-variance regression procedures into weak-moment procedures. The reduction is based on empirical residual pruning and is agnostic to the moment exponent, the noise scale, the covariance, and the design moment.
