items.summary: This paper proposes a framework to analyze the effects of counterfactual policies on the unconditional quantiles of an outcome variable. For a given counterfactual policy, we obtain identified sets for the effect of both marginal and global changes in the proportion of treated individuals. To conduct a sensitivity analysis, we introduce the quantile breakdown frontier, a curve that $(i)$ indicates whether a sensitivity analysis is possible or not, and $(ii)$ when a sensitivity analysis is possible, quantifies the amount of selection bias consistent with a given conclusion of interest across different quantiles. To illustrate our method, we perform a sensitivity analysis on the effect of unionizing low income workers on the quantiles of the distribution of (log) wages.

items.title: Shadow economy as a null set. Measure-theoretic approach to shadow economy
items.summary: In this paper we asked if the shadow economy can be defined as a system of null sets for institutional measures or sensors that measure economic transactions. As an answer a measure-theoretic testable framework to redefine and quantify the shadow economy was designed. Traditional economic definitions frequently conflate the actual shadow economy with the observational limitations of state institutions. To resolve this, we model the shadow economy as a null set relative to institutional measures and analyze three complementary economic regimes. We explore in this context how standard mathematical tools can be given economic meaning. First, in the low-resolution regime, we apply Banach Lattices and Lebesgue decomposition of a measure to address transaction underreporting by aggregating incomplete institutional registries using a supremum fusion operator. Second, for hidden economic dimensions, we utilize Copula theory and Kullback-Leibler divergence optimization to reconstruct unobserved financial flows from technological and physical indicators. Third, we address audit scalability by modeling the shadow economy as a sparse vector, applying Compressed Sensing to detect high-volume sparse evasion networks through random, incoherent, and privacy-preserving sampling.

items.title: Analytical modelling of compliance dynamics under fiscal feedback: tipping thresholds, intervention costs and hysteresis
items.summary: Compliance with taxes and other collective obligations is often enforced with resources that come from those who comply, so that non-compliance erodes its own deterrent. We develop an exactly solvable dynamical model of compliance under this fiscal feedback. Individuals choose between paying and evading by imitating those who do better, and the budget against evasion is a share of the revenue, split between enforcement and education. The model yields closed-form expressions for the equilibria, the tipping thresholds and their bifurcations, the budgets needed to maintain compliance and to restore it after a collapse, and the recovery time near the threshold. Fiscal feedback alone does not produce tipping points: hysteresis appears only when an instrument that changes individual incentives, such as fines or education, is funded by the tax base. Stronger sanctions reduce both the maintenance and the rescue budget, but beyond a critical level they make the system bistable, so that the choice of sanction is a trade-off between efficiency and resilience, which we quantify with a resilience indicator and a resilience-constrained design problem. The cheapest allocation of the budget between enforcement and education is also obtained in closed form. A sensitivity analysis identifies the parameters that control prevention and recovery costs, and stochastic simulations of individual agents and a slow budget cycle confirm the analytical predictions. The framework provides quantitative guidelines for allocating scarce intervention resources in tax compliance and in other enforcement problems with similar feedbacks.

items.title: Social Learning with Selective Sampling
items.summary: This paper studies social learning when some types of actions are more likely to be sampled by successors than others. We show that Bayesian agents can achieve learning even without expanding observations, because the endogenous observation network itself carries information and agents can correct for selection bias. For nonanonymous sampling, we establish sufficient and pairwise necessary conditions of the sampling procedure for learning, which coincide in the binary state-matching model to yield an exact characterization. We also show that stationary anonymous sampling permits asymptotic learning, as agents can correct for selection bias using inverse-probability weighting. Finally, we demonstrate that asymptotic learning can fail under arbitrarily small misspecification of the sampling procedure.

items.title: Neighbourhood flood damage amplifies mortgage default cascades
items.summary: Floods threaten mortgage repayment by damaging homes, disrupting incomes, and worsening conditions in surrounding neighbourhoods. However, it remains unclear how these neighbourhood effects turn local damage into systemic mortgage distress, as Europe's housing crisis leaves households that lose their homes with few affordable alternatives. Using an agent-based model calibrated to Limburg, the Netherlands, we show that damage to surrounding properties can trigger mortgage defaults among households that can still afford to pay, including those whose own homes remain undamaged. In the most severe flood scenario, the annual foreclosure rate more than doubles. As each foreclosure lowers the value of nearby homes, it triggers a cascade. Floods make such large foreclosure cascades more frequent, with the share of foreclosures that belong to these cascades rising from 31% to 45%. They also shift foreclosures towards younger mortgages, when more debt is still outstanding. These findings show how neighbourhood damage extends mortgage risk beyond directly flooded homes and causes foreclosures to arrive in concentrated waves earlier in repayment.

items.title: Probability-Feasible Historical Transport: Sharp Bounds and Falsification Tests for Distributional Pre-Trend Designs
items.summary: Distributional difference-in-differences studies often assume that the post-policy gap between treated and comparison groups is a mixture of pre-policy gaps. This historical-transport assumption can fail in ways that one-statistic checks miss. When policy events are pooled, the average counterfactual can be a valid distribution although no event's counterfactual is, and pooled bounds can exclude the true average effect. Mixtures of past gaps can assign negative probability to outcomes, and cutoff-by-cutoff bounds can be incompatible. We characterize sharp bounds and give breakdown radii, a grid-free confidence region, and tests with and without an experiment. The tests reject transport in the National Supported Work data and expose impossible state counterfactuals behind a pooled minimum-wage bound. For the 1993 Earned Income Tax Credit expansion they pass through 1995, when bounds put single mothers' employment gain relative to childless women at 5 to 7 points; the gain stays positive after dropping early welfare-waiver states.

items.title: Identification of Heterogeneous Peer Effects
items.summary: We develop a peer effects model in which each peer's influence depends on their outcome rank within the peer group. Unlike existing models, it allows non-monotonic effects across ranks. The model admits a unique equilibrium, and its parameters can be identified using peers' exogenous characteristics. We introduce a parsimonious quantile-dependent specification and develop a specification test to guide model selection. Applying the model to student outcomes in Add Health reveals heterogeneous, often non-monotonic spillovers. Counterfactual analysis shows that allowing for non-monotonic peer effects changes the rankings of influential students relative to existing models. Our R package, QuantilePeer, implements these methods.

items.title: How to Mismatch Consumers
items.summary: Should a platform show all consumers all products, or at least those they like most? Or could it raise consumer surplus by mismatching some consumers: showing them only less-preferred products or even excluding them from trade? I show that in both monopoly and duopoly, mismatching can raise aggregate consumer surplus by inducing lower prices. In duopoly, consumer-optimal matching uses a cutoff policy: along each diagonal of equal valuation differences, consumers with lower valuations are matched only to less-preferred products, and some may subsequently be excluded. With independent uniform valuations, this raises aggregate consumer surplus by about 41% over full matching.

items.title: Ancestral origins of environmental (in)attention
items.summary: How do ancestral climate experiences shape today's attitudes towards environmental issues? Combining multiple contemporary surveys and ethnic group-level cultural records with a model of cultural selection on costly attention, we show that ancestral climate anomalies have a lasting U-shaped effect on environmental concern. Descendants of groups exposed to the most regular and the most anomalous climates attach greater importance to the environment, with a dip in between; a pattern mirrored in cultural narratives. But why should contemporary environmental concern remain anchored in ancestral climates when lessons about the value of environmental attention can be learned beyond the conditions in which they were initially acquired? Our model shows that because attention is chosen before conditions are realized, cultural selection rewards perceptions that perform well on average without fully correcting their accuracy across conditions. Ancestral climates can thus leave lasting imprints, even as their influence weakens when environments change. The combination of motives to exploit typical conditions and to protect against extremes gives rise to the U-shape, reconciling anthropological accounts that tie environmental concern to regular and to anomalous climates.

items.title: Linear Demand Systems are Consistent with Discrete Choice
items.summary: Aggregate linear demand systems can be micro-founded by a population of heterogeneous consumers making discrete choices. They can also be extended to incorporate income effects. I prove these results and show how to structurally estimate this class of models using only market-level data. The distribution of heterogeneous consumer preferences is recovered by disciplining the corner solutions with aggregate terms only. This approach allows for the same richness of Berry, Levinsohn, and Pakes (1995) [BLP] while retaining the analytical and computational advantages of linear demand: it does not require exogenously fixing market size, allows for heterogeneity in choice sets, and results in a flexible substitution matrix which varies endogenously as different consumers enter/exit the market. The discrete-choice microfoundation facilitates welfare analysis and the flexible measurement of markups an cost pass-throughs, among a wide range of other applications.

items.title: What the annual energy balance hides: the coordination value of digital platforms for positive energy districts
items.summary: Positive energy districts (PEDs) are usually assessed by annual net energy, whereas distribution networks operate hour by hour. An annually positive district still imports on low-generation hours and exports or curtails on high-generation hours. How large this hourly imbalance is behind an annual balance, and how much of it coordination among prosumers can close without new physical capacity, is not established. This paper models a multi-carrier prosumer community coupling electricity and heat behind a shared grid connection with a net-export hosting limit. The model is solved as a centralized community problem and as a price-taking peer-to-peer (P2P) market. Under convexity, the equilibrium implements the regularized community optimum and the P2P and congestion prices are the duals of the pool-clearing and hosting constraints. The model is calibrated to six European district archetypes with constructed hourly profiles. Hourly self-sufficiency is only 48-50% in the four deeply studied districts and ranges from 48-55% across all six, leaving a no-platform coordination gap of 2.8-5.9% of no-platform economic cost. The shared-forecast step recovers only 6-18% of the gap, while grid-aware pricing reduces curtailment by 45% in the primary district. Coordination mainly reduces surplus-side inefficiency, whereas closing the deficit side requires storage. The results are scenario-based projections for calibrated archetypes, and the operating benefit is small and contingent on binding hosting limits and high feed-in remuneration. For regulators and distribution system operators this supports hourly, bidirectional indicators alongside the annual positive-energy target, and a congestion charge active only in binding hours with a predetermined refund, while the business case for a platform at district scale rests on grid-side value and aggregation across districts.

items.title: A Simple Proof of Koray's Theorem
items.summary: In this note, I provide a direct and self-contained proof of Koray's (2000) theorem, by which a neutral and unanimous social choice function is universally self-selective if and only if it is dictatorial. Koray's (2000) original proof relies on results by Sen (1970) and Houthakker (1950) to construct a social welfare function for each alternative set. He then shows that these functions are Paretian and independent of irrelevant alternatives, allowing him to apply Arrow's (1950, 1951) impossibility theorem. Instead, I construct a cyclic preference profile and show that the voter who ranks the chosen alternative first is the dictator on every finite nonempty alternative set.

items.title: Bayesian Rational Search Engine User
items.summary: A user faces a list ordered by a noisy proxy for relevance and decides whether to pay to inspect another item or stop with the best she has found. Because she does not know the page's quality, each inspection both produces a candidate and updates her beliefs about the remaining items. We show that the optimal policy is a standout rule: the user stops when her best find is sufficiently good relative to what she expects from the page, with the required margin changing with depth. The browsing dynamics collapse to a one-dimensional Markov chain, yielding the full distribution of inspection depth through a closed-form recursion. The model uncovers three reasons for stopping: trust, commit, and cut-losses, and yields testable implications. It also turns inspection depth into a learning-to-rank likelihood. Observed depth restricts the latent relevance path to a polyhedron of survival inequalities, while conversion identifies the terminal winner. Simulations show that the estimator recovers relevance under correct specification and improves ranking using only the incumbent ranker's features. Applied to public Baidu search logs, the inspection depth likelihood produces rankings that align more closely with expert relevance judgments than click-trained alternatives.

items.title: Time-Varying Quantile VAR Models: Estimation and Inference
items.summary: We develop an econometric framework for impulse response analysis in time-varying quantile vector autoregressive (TV-QVAR) models. Unlike standard conditional-mean setting, TV-QVAR systems face a fundamental analytical challenge: neither time-varying parameters nor conditional quantiles propagate linearly through dynamic recursions. To overcome this, we establish a uniform Bahadur representation for local quantile VAR estimation, propose a smoothed check-function approach for tractable parameter inference, and introduce the best linear projection of the time-varying quantile impulse response (TV-QIR) function to recover well-defined dynamic causal effects. Applying our methodology to U.S. industrial production growth and credit spreads from 1919 to 2025 uncovers pronounced structural shifts in tail interdependence, showing that downside asymmetry is concentrated at short horizons and diminishes as the forecast horizon lengthens.

items.title: Coupling and Maximal Inequalities for Graph-Dependent Empirical Processes
items.summary: We develop maximal inequalities for empirical processes indexed by graph-dependent observations. Our bounds separate the complexity of the indexing class from two features specific to graph dependence: the geometry of the underlying graph and the cost of coupling graph-separated blocks to independent copies. The coupling construction combines a novel graph-adapted dependence coefficient with a coloring of a block partition. As an application, we derive Glivenko--Cantelli results and characterize the associated effective sample size. A central implication is that graph-dependent empirical processes need not exhibit a generic root-$n$ rate: convergence is jointly determined by function-class complexity, graph geometry, and the decay of dependence with graph distance. We specialize the results to graphs with polynomial and exponential growth and to directed dyadic graphs. Finally, we apply the results to network autoregressive models, nonlinear local-propagation models, and treatment-interference settings.

items.title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.

items.title: Quadratic Forms of Multivariate $t$-Distributions
items.summary: This paper concerns quadratic forms of multivariate $t$-distributions. This paper derives the joint distribution and density of multiple quadratic forms, and establishes the possibility of a finite series approximation to the CDF. The paper also provides closed-form expressions for all the mixed moments that exist. Inverses of quadratic forms and ratios of quadratic forms are also considered.

items.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Forecast Treatment Effects in Economics?
items.summary: I use LLMs to forecast treatment effects from pre-registrations and pre-analysis plans, evaluating forecasts against results released after the models' cut-off dates. The screened sample includes 1,459 questions from 36 papers. For the most recent time period and model, the median absolute error is 0.053 SD, the average absolute error is 0.098 SD, and the MSE is 0.021, falling to 0.015 after adjusting for sampling variance where standard errors are available. Forecasts substantially outperform benchmarks predicting zero or other papers' mean effects. These results suggest considerable scope for forecasts to inform policy and research.

items.title: DeepVoting: Learning and Improving Voting Rules with Fine-Tuning
items.summary: Recently, social choice theory has been found broadly useful for AI alignment and evaluation, often based on the axiomatic properties for combining preferences provided by social choice functions. However, for many sets of axioms, functions which never violate the axioms are known to not exist, e.g., Arrow's Impossibility Theorem. Recent work on learning novel rules to minimize axiom violations shows the effectiveness of machine learning but explores a limited class of axioms. In this work we show the effectiveness of standard social choice data structures as features for learning existing voting rules, resulting in networks that have better accuracy than past approaches while using an order of magnitude fewer parameters. Subsequently, we develop a process for adding axiomatic properties to existing voting rules. By building novel axiomatic loss functions we are able to use transfer learning to fine-tune existing voting rules in a way that quantitatively preserves their original behaviour while also exhibiting strong adherence to previously absent axiomatic properties, resulting in novel voting rules that are closer to the impossibility frontier than those in the machine learning or theoretical literature.

items.title: Risk aversion with two risks for state-dependent utilities
items.summary: In this paper, we introduce the concept of Arrow-Pratt risk aversion within a two-attribute, state-dependent utility framework, where a primary risk is accompanied by a background risk. Within this setting, we investigate the interrelationships among risk aversion toward one risk in the presence of another risk, the structure of state-dependent two-attribute utility functions, and the degree of correlation between the two risks. More specifically, we establish conditions on the state-dependent two-attribute utility function under which risk aversion toward primary risk is preserved when a background risk is involved, considering various correlation structures between the two types of risks. Additionally, a new concept, uniform risk aversion in the presence of a background risk, is introduced. We show that the above established conditions on the state-dependent two-attribute utility function are equivalent to uniform risk aversion toward primary risk in presence of a background risk. These findings offer new insights into state-dependent preferences for correlated risks. Two applications in the contexts of fair insurance contract and optimal prevention within a two-period model illustrate the practical usefulness of the proposed risk aversion with two risks under state-dependent utilities.

items.title: Uniform Inference for Parameters Identified by Conditional Quantile Restrictions
items.summary: Many structural and dynamic economic models imply that key parameters are identified by conditional quantile restrictions. Building on the exponential weighting approach of Bierens (1990) and the penalized maximum statistics of Chen et al. (2025), we develop a uniform inference method for such parameters. We construct an adaptive $\ell_1$-penalized statistic from a process indexed by quantiles and weighting directions. The statistic aggregates evidence across quantiles and regularizes maximization over directions. A shifted bootstrap is used to estimate local power for penalty selection. Under the stated conditions, adaptive selection asymptotically preserves or improves worst case local power relative to the unpenalized test over a prespecified set of alternatives. The improvement is strict when a positive candidate penalty raises the population level criterion above its value at zero. We also extend the process and bootstrap theory to the setting with pre-estimated nuisance parameters. We characterize their contribution to the limiting process, correct the variance estimator, and establish Gaussian multiplier bootstrap validity for null inference. Monte Carlo experiments favor the CvM-KS method for size control under pre-estimation and show that adaptive penalization can improve empirical power relative to the unpenalized test.

items.title: The Uniqueness of Exponential Second-Order Expected Utility
items.summary: A decision-maker entertains several probability models of the state of the world, distrusts each of them, and is unsure which of them holds. She therefore carries two relative-entropy penalties: one on departures from a given model and one on departures from the reference she places on models. The literature that introduced this structure treats the equality of the two penalty parameters as a tractable special case. We show that it is in fact a necessary and sufficient condition: her criterion carries a single relative-entropy penalty if and only if the two parameters agree, that is, when she charges the same price for doubting a model as for doubting her weights on models. Under that one condition the two layers collapse: the criterion is an exponential second-order expected utility based at the Bayesian predictive distribution, for every compact model set and every prior, with no large-sample limit anywhere. When the condition fails, the caution she displays blends her two parameters, with a weight equal to the share of an act's predictive variance that comes from disagreement among the models; since that share varies across acts, no single parameter and baseline represent her, and the same variation identifies the two parameters separately. The exponential aggregator and relative entropy are each forced: no other continuous and strictly increasing aggregator delivers the collapse, and within the power-divergence family only relative entropy does.

items.title: The AI Layoff Trap
items.summary: If AI displaces workers faster than the economy can reabsorb them, it risks eroding the consumer demand firms depend on. We show that knowing this is not enough for firms to stop it. In a competitive task-based economy, each firm captures the full cost saving from automation but bears only a fraction of the demand loss it creates in the product market; the rest falls on rivals. This demand externality traps rational firms in an automation arms race, displacing workers beyond what is collectively optimal. The mechanism harms both workers and firm owners and can survive in general equilibrium. More competition and higher AI productivity can amplify the excess. Wage adjustment, free entry, transfers, worker equity, and Coasean bargaining need not eliminate it. A Pigouvian automation tax implements the cooperative optimum. Policy should address not only the aftermath of automation but also the competitive incentives driving it.

items.title: Robust Signal Maximization in Spillover Experiments
items.summary: We study the optimal design and analysis of experiments for estimating spillover effects. Assuming a known (e.g., linear) exposure mapping, we characterize the treatment-assignment distribution and regression-based estimator that minimize worst-case approximate variance against a broad class of distributions of unobservables. The design problem yields an intuitive solution in which the planner trades off spillover signal strength against dispersion of spillover variation. The analysis problem yields a simple recentered instrumental variable estimator to best leverage this variation. This framework produces natural solutions in several benchmark cases - such as clustered exposure - and suggests computationally tractable approximations for general networks, including bipartite settings. We illustrate these new tools in semi-synthetic experiments based on three applications from development economics. Our approach yields large standard error reductions in these experiments, increasing effective sample sizes by 44-266%.

items.title: Logarithmic Tracing and Equilibrium Selection in Asymmetric Coordination Games
items.summary: We study equilibrium selection in asymmetric pure coordination games with finitely many players and actions. A logarithmic regularization defines a tracing-type path of interior equilibria from the uniform strategy profile. We reduce the equilibrium conditions to single-peaked scalar functions and show that, when one associated payoff index is uniquely minimal, the connected equilibrium branch from the uniform profile converges to the corresponding coordinated outcome. With two players, this condition is equivalent to maximizing the sum of square-root payoffs, extending the known two-action result to finitely many actions. A three-player example shows that the square-root rule does not generally extend to more players.

items.title: A short way to stability
items.summary: The paper presents a concise and straightforward approach way to obtain the basic facts about stable contract systems in bilateral markets: existence, polariza- tion, and lattice structure. The primary tool employed is the notion of desirability operator. This notion is essentially equivalent to the concept of Plott choice function, but it allows for a clearer visualization of stable systems of contracts as fixed points of some operator. The existence and other properties of these fixed points is obtained using Knaster-Tarski fixed-point theorem. Additionally, we explore related topics such as order structure of the set of stable contract systems, the polarization of the interests of the parties, the constructiveness of the approach, its application to comparative statics, a relaxation of bipartition assumption, as well as generalization to systems where contracts can be established with varying intensities instead of being either accepted or denied.

items.title: Decision Theory with Degree of Membership in the State Space
items.summary: Classical decision theory considers a decision maker (DM) who faces a choice set C and believes that the true state of nature s* lies in a state space S. An objective function w(., .): C x S -> R1 maps actions and states into welfare. The DM wants to maximize w(., s*) but does not know s*. The state space specifies a labeled set of possible states. Possibility is binary: every state in S is possible and no state outside of S is possible. Thinking that this binary perspective on possibility is too rigid, we generalize the classical theory. We begin with a universe of labeled states U and a residual unlabeled state r. Classical theory associates a binary possibility indicator mu(s) with each s in (U, r). The residual state r is not possible, so mu(r) = 0. The state space is S = [s in U: mu(s) = 1]. We expand the range of mu to be the interval [0, 1]. Thus, mu is now a real number measuring degree of membership, a term we adopt from fuzzy set theory. The membership function mu(.): (U, r) -> [0, 1] differs substantively from but is consistent with the subjective probability distributions of Bayesian decision theory. Bayesian theory places a subjective distribution on the elements of a classical state space, each of whose members has degree of membership one. Degree of membership expresses the distinct idea that a DM may want to quantitatively express uncertainty regarding the composition of the state space. A mathematical distinction between subjective probabilities and degrees of membership is that the former must sum to one, but the latter need not. After formalizing basic ideas, we extend three prominent classical decision criteria--maximization of subjective expected welfare, minimax regret, and maximin--to our generalization of classical decision theory.

items.title: Social choice with transfers
items.summary: We consider the problem of social choice when transfers between agents are possible. This includes several canonical applications: public-good provision, management of a common resource, settlement of debts, and division of goods. The question of interest is, given a set of possible alternatives, which should be chosen and what transfers, if any, should be made? We show that the Shapley value of the stand-alone game is the only solution to satisfy certain desirable properties.

items.title: Incentivizing Information Acquisition
items.summary: I study a principal-agent model in which a principal hires an agent to collect information about an unknown continuous state. The agent acquires a signal whose distribution is centered around the state, controlling the signal's precision at a cost. The principal observes neither the precision nor the signal, but rather, using transfers that can depend on the state, incentivizes the agent to choose high precision and report the signal truthfully. I identify a sufficient and necessary condition on the agent's information structure which ensures that there exists an optimal transfer with a simple cutoff structure: the agent receives a fixed prize when his prediction is close enough to the state and receives nothing otherwise. This condition is mild and applies to all signal distributions commonly used in the literature.

items.title: When the Scaffold Stays On: AI, Practice Style, and Screening in Elite Skill Formation
items.summary: Generative AI can perform many of the tasks through which programmers build skill. When it substitutes for practice, skill development suffers; when it complements practice, learning may accelerate. Therefore, one programmer in the substitute mode and another in the complement mode can produce the same AI-assisted output yet differ in the skill they have acquired. We ask what digital practice records reveal about skill formation and whether AI-prohibited evaluations help distinguish the two modes of AI use. We follow 10,419 users of Codeforces (CF), an open, unproctored programming practice and contest platform with no enforced restriction on AI assistance, from 2018 to 2025. We link them to the rosters of the International Collegiate Programming Contest (ICPC) and the International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI), which admit entrants through qualification rounds and prohibit AI under in-person proctoring. From CF practice telemetry, we construct an AI-prompt signature (higher first-attempt acceptance rates, fewer attempts per solved problem, and fewer rapid debugging retries), consistent with AI-assisted practice. Three patterns emerge. Practice shifted toward the signature across entry cohorts spanning the releases of GitHub Copilot and ChatGPT. On CF, a stronger signature is associated with slower skill growth among users not linked to ICPC or IOI rosters, but not among roster-linked users. Among AI-era entrants who reached ICPC, larger within-user shifts toward the signature are positively associated with non-AI performance. These patterns are consistent with qualification screening on acquired skill, which admits users who complement practice with AI and excludes those who substitute AI for practice.

items.title: Echoes of the boom in hydraulic fracturing: What changes in Louisiana's energy complex reveal about global energy cycles
items.summary: The expansion of hydraulic fracturing (i.e. fracking) led to global shifts in energy markets that were felt acutely along the US Gulf Coast and particularly in the state of Louisiana. This article presents a data-focused examination of trends in the energy industry, and shows how they led to potentially counterintuitive, negative impacts in Louisiana's economy. Most notably, hydraulic fracturing led to a massive expansion in oil and gas supplies that contributed to a significant decline in oil prices in late 2014, contributing to significant job losses. Louisiana's economic downturns were tied to global shifts in energy markets that had major geostrategic implications. More broadly, results indicate that large and long period cycles in the supply, demand and price of oil can have widespread impacts on job creation and loss. In states like Louisiana with a large and diversified energy complex, the impacts of these trends can be highly uneven. One impact in the 21st Century appears to be highly concentrated areas of industrial development within a broader pattern of regional economic decline. Furthermore, trends identified in this study suggest the potential for the emergence of major cycles in the gas market. Whereas natural gas was previously mostly transported by pipelines and sold through long-term contracts, the emergence of liquified natural gas creates the potential for more volatile gas market dynamics. The implications of gas market cycles, while not yet known, could be of major economic significance.

items.title: Measuring Colombia's Informal Output: Relative Earnings and Identification in a Bayesian Two-Sector Model, 1993-2026
items.summary: How much of Colombia's measured output is produced by informal work? The answer cannot be read from the labor-informality rate: Colombia combines an informality rate above 50% with a much smaller informal share of output, because informal work is less productive. We estimate a Bayesian two-sector business-cycle model on quarterly national accounts and on reconstructed employment and informality series for 1993-2026. Identification comes from a new quarterly series of informal-to-formal labor earnings built from household-survey microdata for 2007-2026. Formal production uses capital and labor, informal production is labor based, and an accounting relationship maps relative earnings, the informality rate and the formal capital share into the informal output share. We show that aggregate data alone cannot pin down the size of the informal sector, and that relative earnings identify its quarterly path: from 2007 the path is invariant, within 0.3 percentage points, to the model's steady state. The informal share declines from about 30% of GDP in 1993 to 20% in 2026Q2, while labor informality falls from about 69% to 54%. The estimates lie within the range of published shadow-economy series for Colombia, close to the enhanced MIMIC estimates of Asllani, Dell'Anno and Schneider for 2009-2020. Sensitivity analysis quantifies the role of the capital share and of non-wage labor costs.

items.title: Portfolio Choice of Spouses with Heterogeneous Risk Preferences over Shared Household Consumption
items.summary: A number of recent empirical papers rely on a collective model to analyze the portfolio choice of spouses, their heterogeneous risk preferences, and intra-household bargaining. I show that although Pareto-Efficient, this approach generates a counterintuitive result with constant Pareto weights: an increase in the risk aversion of a household member can lead to an increase in household risk-taking. Moreover, household wealth affects the preferred risky portfolio share even under CRRA preferences and can make the household insensitive to preferences of a spouse. I offer an alternative approach based on the concept of risk premia and show that it always generates a Pareto-efficient and monotonic household level solution. I derive an intuitive normalization to the Pareto weights in the collective model which generates an approximately equivalent solution. Finally, I discuss multiplicative aggregation of utilities previously used in this literature and show that it is also approximately equivalent to the suggested approach.

items.title: Advancing AI Capabilities and Evolving Labor Outcomes
items.summary: This paper examines how labor market outcomes changed across occupations as AI capabilities advanced from chatbots to reasoning models and AI agents. We construct an occupational AI exposure score for each capability stage and relate its change to the Current Population Survey through June 2026. In aggregate, occupations whose exposure rose more did not lose employment or see higher unemployment over three years. However, the number of workers under 30 in these occupations fell by about 8 percent per standard deviation of the exposure change, and the decline is concentrated among young workers without a college degree and in office and customer service occupations rather than in technical occupations. Their unemployment did not rise, consistent with less entry rather than more layoffs. College graduates aged 30 to 49 gained full-time positions in the same occupations, so the workforce in exposed occupations became older and more educated. The same comparisons for 2017 to 2022 show no such patterns.

items.title: Science under Threat? A Natural Experiment in Economics
items.summary: Academic freedom is under strain worldwide. To study how scholars respond to (perceived) political pressure, we exploit a natural experiment in the United States: the publication in early 2025 of a "stop list" of words flagged by the government. We find that economists at universities relying more on federal funding reduce gender-, race-, and environment-related content with flagged words relative to other US and UK economists. Regarding mechanisms, our analyses suggest that self-censorship may explain this reduction better than direct grant cancellation. Estimates are similar when excluding papers acknowledging federal funding or controlling for universities' institutional measures and financial distress.

items.title: Bayesian Persuasion without Commitment
items.summary: We introduce a model of persuasion in which a sender without any commitment power privately gathers information about an unknown state of the world and then chooses what to verifiably disclose to a receiver. The receiver does not know how many experiments the sender is able to run, and may therefore be uncertain as to whether the sender disclosed all of her information. Despite this challenge, we show that, under general conditions, the sender is able to achieve the same payoff as in the full-commitment Bayesian persuasion case.

items.title: Normative Ceilings and Stochastic Giving
items.summary: People randomize when they allocate money to others, and what else is available changes how they randomize: adding an alternative can raise the probability that an existing one is chosen, in violation of Regularity. We characterize a model of stochastic choice in which a selfish decision maker faces norm-driven social pressure and the menu matters only through one scalar, the normative ceiling, defined as the most pro-social alternative available. We introduce two conditions on cross-menu comparisons: comparisons line up through a single rescaling attached to each menu's most normative alternative, and higher normative levels are more selective. Together with standard positivity, continuity, acyclicity, order and richness requirements, these conditions force the randomization cost to depend on the menu only through the ceiling. Raising the ceiling makes the cost uniformly more curved. Random utility and baseline perturbed utility models imply Regularity; models of deliberate randomization necessarily violate it; ours does neither. Instead, our model predicts that Regularity can fail only when the ceiling rises across behaviorally distinguishable levels, and that it then fails at the least selfish alternatives. This prediction is a sign restriction with no free parameters, and we show how nested menus test it.

items.title: Learning Where to Look: The Geometry of Data Combination and Collection
items.summary: Large datasets covering populations in the status quo are becoming increasingly available, while interventions can usually be rolled out only to small selected samples. How can these two sources of information be combined to estimate the effect on untreated units? And who should be treated next to improve estimation the most? I focus on matching estimators and shed light on both problems, drawing from results in computational geometry. First, I prove that interpolation over the Delaunay simplex minimizes worst-case bias at any untreated unit, given any treated sample. Second, I show the collection problem has a geometric representation that yields significant reductions in worst-case bias with few additions (80% with 20 additions in an empirical application), leading to sizeable cost-efficiency gains in collection plans.

items.title: Exchange rights and vacancy priorities
items.summary: Many institutions let incumbents exchange positions while allocating announced vacancies by priority, withdrawing positions released by vacancy recipients. A policy specifies permitted exchanges, vacancy eligibility, and priorities. A strategy-proof, individually rational rule protecting exchange rights and vacancy priorities exists precisely for policies without conflict cycles. Restricting protection to first choices does not enlarge this class. We introduce the propose-and-trade rule, which satisfies these properties and selects the applicant-optimal core allocation under every conflict-free policy. We identify when propose-and-trade is the unique strategy-proof, individually rational rule protecting first choices. These axioms characterize deferred acceptance and top trading cycles in their classic settings. Under a policy with a conflict cycle, propose-and-trade is manipulable but protects exchange rights and first-choice claims. Replacing it with any strategy-proof rule makes some applicant worse off at some profile. We show when priority reform alone can eliminate conflict cycles and when eligibility or exchange permissions must change.

items.title: Rethinking Arrow--Debreu: A New Framework for Exchange
items.summary: This paper revisits the Arrow--Debreu general equilibrium framework through the lens of effective trade, emphasizing the distinction between theoretical and realizable market interactions. We develop the Effective Trade Model (ETM), where transactions arise from bilateral feasibility rather than aggregate supply and demand desires. Within this framework, we establish the main properties of the price-demand correspondence and prove the existence of Nash equilibria, incorporating production, money, and network topology. Our results show that equilibrium is shaped by transaction constraints, subjective pricing, and decentralized negotiation, rather than by universal market-clearing conditions, and thereby call into question the foundations of welfare theory.

items.title: Inference for Linear Systems with Unknown Coefficients
items.summary: This paper considers the problem of testing whether there exists a solution satisfying known linear constraints to a linear system of equations. Importantly and in contrast to some prior work, we allow all parameters in the system of equations, including the slope coefficients, to be unknown. For this reason, we describe the linear system as having unknown (as opposed to known) coefficients. This hypothesis testing problem arises naturally when constructing confidence sets for possibly partially identified parameters in the analysis of nonparametric instrumental variables models, treatment effect models, and random coefficient models, among other settings. We begin our analysis by providing a novel characterization of the set of coefficient pairs for which the linear system is feasible. Leveraging this characterization, we develop a testing procedure based on sample splitting. We establish its validity under weak and interpretable conditions on the linear system. An important feature of these conditions is that they permit the dimensionality of the problem to grow rapidly with the sample size. A further attractive property of our test is that it does not require simulation to compute suitable critical values. We illustrate the practical relevance of our theoretical results in a simulation study.

items.title: AI, Specialization, and the Organization of Knowledge Work: Evidence from Legal Services
items.summary: Artificial intelligence makes specialized knowledge cheaper to use, but its effects on professional-service firms depend on how clients reallocate work and how suppliers respond. We develop a framework linking individual self-provision, enterprise make-or-buy decisions, and pricing by specialist firms. As AI improves lower-priced alternatives, clients may reallocate work across outside providers without bringing it in-house. If the departing work is more price-sensitive than the work that remains, premium firms may raise their optimal markups even as their share of work declines. We examine these margins in U.S. legal services. Across 89 federal districts, a difference-in-differences analysis finds a 6.6-percentage-point increase in non-prisoner self-representation relative to prisoner petitions by fiscal 2025, remaining substantial after adjusting for pre-existing trends. In contrast, lawyer employment shows no clear post-2022 shift toward client firms. Legal-AI benchmarks reveal continuing limitations in reliably completing complex, multi-step work, offering one possible explanation. Meanwhile, the largest law firms reported 13% revenue growth in 2025 despite nearly flat billable hours, while lower-priced firms experienced stronger demand growth. Reported AI integration is also stronger among firms with lower revenue per lawyer. These patterns highlight the importance of changes in work allocation and supplier competition, even as much of the underlying reallocation predates generative AI. The findings illustrate why cheaper expertise need not produce either widespread internalization or declining prices for premium professional services.

items.title: The Rural Margin of Territorial Peace: Within-Municipality Evidence from Colombia
items.summary: Colombia's peace agreement introduced participatory development programs and congressional constituencies reserved for conflict victims with a rural electorate. I use repeated waves of the Social Capital Barometer and a triple-difference event study to compare changes in rural-urban engagement gaps in municipalities covered by both reforms with those elsewhere. Rural engagement evolved more favorably relative to urban engagement in the covered municipalities. The index captures coordination around shared problems, civic participation and party linkage, with coordination providing the clearest evidence. The result persists when the reference period precedes the agreement and the baseline wave is excluded. Program activity and organizational membership patterns are consistent with participatory investment and political mobilization. The findings document a change in engagement beyond voting under the joint territorial reforms.

items.title: Keeping in Place After the Storm-Emergency Assistance and Evictions
items.summary: We offer evidence that federal emergency assistance (FEMA) in the days following natural disasters mitigate evictions in comparison to similar emergency scenarios where FEMA aid is not provided. We find an approximate 10.9% increase in overall evictions after hurricane natural disaster events driven in large part by areas in close proximity of the hurricane path that do not receive FEMA rental assistance. Furthermore, we also show that FEMA aid acts as a liquidity buffer to other forms of emergency credit, specifically we find that overall transactions volumes decrease during hurricane events in locations that do receive FEMA aid. This effect largely reverses in areas that do not receive FEMA aid. Overall, this suggests that the availability of emergency liquidity during natural disaster events is indeed a binding constraint with real household financial consequences, in particular through our documented channel of evictions and in usage of high-cost credit.

items.title: Designing Algorithmic Recommendations to Achieve Human-AI Complementarity
items.summary: Algorithms frequently assist, rather than replace, human decision-makers. However, the design and analysis of algorithms often focus on predicting outcomes and do not explicitly model their effect on human decisions. This discrepancy between the design and role of algorithmic assistants becomes particularly concerning in light of empirical evidence that suggests that algorithmic assistants again and again fail to improve human decisions. In this article, we formalize the design of recommendation algorithms that assist human decision-makers without making restrictive ex-ante assumptions about how recommendations affect decisions. We formulate an algorithmic-design problem that leverages the potential-outcomes framework from causal inference to model the effect of recommendations on a human decision-maker's binary treatment choice. Within this model, we make a connection between algorithmic recommendations and instrumental variables. Leveraging this connection, we introduce a monotonicity assumption that leads to an intuitive classification of human responses to the algorithm. Under this assumption, we can express the human's response to algorithmic recommendations in terms of their compliance with the algorithm and the active decision they would take if the algorithm sends no recommendation. We showcase the utility of our framework using an online experiment that simulates a hiring task. We argue that our approach can make sense of the relative performance of different recommendation algorithms in the experiment and can help design solutions that realize human-AI complementarity. Finally, we leverage our approach to derive maximin-optimal recommendation algorithms that can be implemented with machine learning using limited training data.

items.title: A Bayesian latent class reinforcement learning framework to capture adaptive, feedback-driven travel behaviour
items.summary: Many travel decisions involve a degree of experience formation, where individuals learn their preferences over time. At the same time, there is extensive scope for heterogeneity across individual travellers, both in their underlying preferences and in how these evolve. The present paper puts forward a Latent Class Reinforcement Learning (LCRL) model that allows analysts to capture both of these phenomena. We apply the model to a driving simulator dataset and estimate the parameters through Variational Bayes. We identify three distinct classes of individuals that differ markedly in how they adapt their preferences: the first displays context-dependent preferences with context-specific exploitative tendencies; the second follows a persistent exploitative strategy regardless of context; and the third engages in an exploratory strategy combined with context-specific preferences.

items.title: Entry Deterrence with Public Signals: Revisiting the Chain-Store Paradox
items.summary: We revisit the classic chain-store paradox by introducing exogenous public signals about the incumbent's private type that arrive each period over a finite horizon. We fully characterize perfect Bayesian equilibria in terms of sequences of reputation cutoffs that increase over time: entrants enter below their cutoff, while the normal incumbent mixes below its cutoff and fights above it. The equilibrium outcome is generically unique. Information arrival dampens the incentive to build a reputation, so full deterrence need not emerge as the horizon grows arbitrarily long, even when the incumbent is very patient. We characterize exactly when there is full deterrence in the limit, along with the limiting equilibrium when there is not.

items.title: Inference in dynamic models for panel data using the moving block bootstrap
items.summary: Inference in linear panel data models is complicated by the presence of fixed effects when (some of) the regressors are not strictly exogenous. Under asymptotics where the number of cross-sectional observations and time periods grow at the same rate, the within-group estimator is consistent but its limit distribution features a bias term. In this paper we show that a panel version of the moving block bootstrap, where blocks of adjacent cross-sections are resampled with replacement, replicates the limit distribution of the within-group estimator. Confidence ellipsoids and hypothesis tests based on the reverse-percentile bootstrap are thus asymptotically valid without the need to take the presence of bias into account.

items.title: Interpreting the Morbidity Gap
items.summary: The Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study now reports the morbidity gap (MG), life expectancy minus healthy life expectancy, as an indicator in its own right. Writing MG as the expected cumulative rate of years lived with disability (YLDs) at the life-table age at death, we use stochastic dominance results to show what MG measures, how it responds to mortality and how it relates to the YLDs of the current population. We show the following. (a) A YLD profile gives an MG no larger than another's under every life table if and only if its cumulative YLD rate is nowhere higher. (b) With YLD rates fixed, lower mortality at every age widens MG, so that removing a risk factor that raises mortality reduces MG by less than its contribution to MG in GBD's risk factor attribution. (c) A family of results gives easily interpretable conditions on the age structure of the population for the crude YLD rate to be above or below the life-table YLD rate, which is MG divided by life expectancy, and these conditions change with population ageing. We illustrate the results for Singapore, where MG widened from 8.9 to 11.2 years between 1990 and 2023.

items.title: Structural economic change under the digital transformation
items.summary: Productivity improvements in digital industries could massively reshape the structure of production networks and drive significant labour reallocation across sectors. We examine these adjustments using a calibrated agent-based model of the global economy. We consider two scenarios with the same cumulative increase in digital-supplier productivity, which differ in how digital inputs in exposed industries are incorporated into production. The key difference is whether digital inputs enter as standard intermediate inputs (low embeddedness) or are combined directly with primary factors (high embeddedness). Across economies, both scenarios generate gains in gross output, household utility, and GDP, although value-added gains are more modest and unevenly distributed across sectors. High embeddedness generally amplifies production responses, particularly in industries highly exposed to digital inputs. Structurally, as digital industries become central in the production network and attract labour from other activities, other industries move further upstream and downstream. Persistent labour reallocation pressures also indicate potential unemployment risks where workers cannot move to expanding industries. These findings stress that, beyond productivity gains derived from advances in digital technologies, economic and social consequences depend on how digital inputs integrate into production and on workers' possibilities to adapt to structural change.

items.title: Multiscale Reconstruction of Weighted Networks from Coarse-Grained Data
items.summary: Network reconstruction from partial information is usually performed at the same resolution level at which constraints are observable. This becomes problematic when only coarse-grained information is available, while the relevant process occurs at a finer scale. Here we employ the multiscale model of weighted networks introduced in a companion paper and turn it into a probabilistic framework for reconstructing weighted networks across arbitrary aggregation levels. The model is built to preserve its functional form under coarse-graining, so that global parameters calibrated on an observable aggregate layer can be transferred to finer layers without refitting. We test the method on two empirical systems with different aggregation mechanisms. In the International Trade Network, countries are aggregated into geographic macro-regions and the observed coarse-grained layer is used to infer the underlying country-level network. In the Dutch production network, sectoral flows are reconstructed across the hierarchical industrial classification, using coarser sectoral layers to infer finer ones. In both geographical and sectoral settings, we benchmark our genuinely multiscale reconstruction method against a state-of-the-art weighted reconstruction model calibrated directly at the target resolution, and therefore using additional information available at the same (finer) scale at which performance is evaluated. Despite this informational disadvantage, our method recovers the fine-scale binary structure with high accuracy, improving precision, specificity, accuracy and maximum degree-error diagnostics, while remaining nearly equivalent in sensitivity.

items.title: An Enforcement Foundation for Constrained Equal Awards
items.summary: Standard claims problems take claims as given. We ask how rule selection changes when a certified claim can be augmented by a privately known component that is costly to verify. In a binary environment, equal treatment of equals, claim boundedness, and efficiency impose a sharp lower bound on the gain from exaggeration and hence on the expected auditing needed for truthful reporting to be weakly dominant. The constrained equal awards (CEA) rule attains this bound at every report profile through a correlated audit policy. Conversely, every profilewise audit-minimal rule is CEA. The pointwise result also makes CEA the unique admissible rule that minimizes expected verification cost under every prior over true claims.

items.title: Selective Verification in Centralized Admissions: Which Priority Claims Must Be Checked?
items.summary: Centralized admissions platforms grant priority based on self-reported facts such as residence, sibling status, or family income, and a false claim can cost another applicant her seat. Verifying every claim before matching is expensive, yet checking only admitted applicants afterward is unsafe: a false claim by an applicant who ends up unmatched may already have triggered a chain of rejections. We show how a platform can check far fewer claims without changing any outcome. A claim matters only if it can move its applicant across a school's admission cutoff, and we give an exact, easily computed test for when this happens. Checking only such claims, and only when they could change a school's tentative choice, reproduces every application, rejection, and assignment of deferred acceptance under full verification. When claims are truthful, checking the highest claimed priority first minimizes checks among such policies at each school decision, and the number of checks never exceeds the school's capacity. Truthful reporting of preferences and eligibility is a weakly dominant strategy, so incentives deliver the conditions under which this audit order is optimal. In simulated markets, the policy cuts verification by 76 percent relative to checking every claim upfront and by 36 percent relative to checking each claim when it first reaches a school. The design principle is to verify decisions, not files.

items.title: Obvious group manipulations in voting
items.summary: We study obvious group manipulation in voting and characterize it as manipulation identifiable from a coalition's option sets alone. Our analysis focuses on two overlapping classes: tops-only rules and rules satisfying the majority criterion, including all Condorcet-consistent rules. On the universal domain with at least three alternatives, a tops-only rule is not obviously manipulable by groups (NOMG) if and only if it is dictatorial. For rules satisfying the majority criterion, NOMG is impossible when $n,m\geq3$, except with four voters and three alternatives. We quantify the coalition sizes behind these restrictions, obtaining sharp bounds for efficient tops-only rules and an exact threshold for majority-criterion rules with odd electorates. In the exceptional configuration, we characterize an interval of NOMG scoring rules containing Borda, which is also Condorcet consistent there. We further characterize NOMG with two alternatives and apply our tops-only characterization to generalized median voter schemes and voting by committees.

items.title: Product Returns and the Value of Search Prominence
items.summary: Ordered-search models typically make prominence valuable because the first-listed seller receives more traffic. We show that product returns can overturn this logic by changing not only the volume but also the composition of demand. We develop a duopoly model in which consumers inspect products sequentially, learn a coarse match signal through search, discover realized taste only after purchase, and may return the product. With positive consumer hassle costs for product returns and a general taste distribution, optimal consumer behavior is characterized by pre-search inspection, post-search purchase, and retention cutoffs. In a low-hassle, full-refund benchmark with uniformly distributed taste values, the non-prominent firm charges a higher price because consumers who reach it are screened by their experience with the prominent product. Although prominence generates more visits and gross orders, it also exposes the first seller to less-screened, more return-prone demand. When seller-side return losses are sufficiently large, the prominent firm can earn less than its rival while both firms earn positive profits. The reversal also persists on local active pricing branches under small positive hassle costs, small departures from full refunds, and finite oligopoly. Sellers' willingness to pay for prominence therefore depends on how a higher ranking changes both the profits from retained sales and the losses on returned units.

items.title: Pragmatic DML with AI-Learned Representations
items.summary: Text, images, and other rich objects increasingly enter causal analysis through AI-learned representations used as controls. For a broad class of estimands, replacing the raw object by its representation shifts the target by the inner product of two errors: one in the outcome regression and one in the balancing weight. The bias is therefore bounded by the product of their sizes. Three consequences follow. With a fixed representation, the usual cross-fitted debiased machine learning (DML) interval is valid for a representation-specific target, and for the causal target when the approximation bias is negligible relative to sampling error. When this bias may not be negligible, a sensitivity analysis bounds the causal target and supplies confidence bounds for the endpoints. When the embedding is tuned on the sample, three approaches preserve valid inference: fixed-menu fine-tuning, joint-loss tuning, and double representation selection. A multimodal demand application illustrates the workflow.

items.title: Globally promoting legumes by production or use subsidies
items.summary: Despite consensus on the positive economic, environmental, and health effects of expanding legume production and consumption, the share of cropland devoted to them remains relatively small, and their share of human consumption is negligible compared with other protein sources such as meat. The presence of externalities associated with legume production and consumption gives room for policy interventions. In this context, we estimate the effects of global subsidies on legume production and consumption using CGEBox, an open-source and open-access Computable General Equilibrium modelling platform, with integrated accounting for land use, land cover, and energy, and considering agricultural and non-agricultural households. The analysis offers high agri-food detail and a special focus on Ghana and Germany, two countries with different agroecological and socioeconomic conditions facing multiple food system issues. Compared to production subsidies, we find that use subsidies are more effective at reducing consumer prices of legumes and stimulating household intake of macronutrients, without displacing consumption of other foods. In contrast, production subsidies are more effective at boosting domestic supply, but also stimulate their feed use. Furthermore, subsidies drive up crop land to the detriment of pasture land and forests. The impact of these subsidies also reveals profound regional disparities, influenced by patterns of land use and of production and consumption.

items.title: Identification and Estimation of Semiparametric Multilayered Sample Selection Models
items.summary: Many selection problems are multilayered, involving both participation and sorting among ordered or unordered categories. Unlike binary selection, in which selection bias can be summarized by a scalar control function, ordered and multinomial sorting generally produce multi-index control functions for which identification depends on both covariate variation and the structure of the selection correction function. I establish identification results for both architectures, showing how nonlinearity in the selection equation can substitute for excluded variables under structural restrictions. I also show how additional structural restrictions reduce the control-function dimension and make estimation practical. I propose $\sqrt{n}$-consistent two-step sieve plug-in estimators and apply the framework to gender wage gaps among Korean college graduates. Under the ordered specification, selection correction substantially narrows the estimated large-firm wage gap.

items.title: Measuring climate credibility? Talk, emissions, and corporate debt composition
items.summary: We examine whether a directional measure that compares emissions growth with earlier climate discussion is associated with corporate debt composition. The analysis links earnings-call climate language, LSEG/Refinitiv emissions, Capital IQ debt shares, RepRisk incidents, and accounting information for public firms over 2010--2021. The Emissions-to-Talk Index (ETI) is the central empirical measure, but we describe it literally rather than treating it as a general indicator of disclosure quality. In the baseline industry-and-year fixed-effect specification, a higher ETI is associated with a lower bank-debt share. The estimate falls by about four-fifths and is statistically insignificant when firm and year fixed effects are used on the same observations. It is also insignificant when the completed index is used to predict debt composition one calendar year later. Results based on the separate talk and emissions components, a ratio-free interaction, and complete talk--emissions categories lead to the same broad conclusion. Oster and Frank sensitivity calculations, alternative covariance estimates, exact year-sign bootstrap calculations, and leave-one-year-out estimates show that the contemporaneous result is sensitive to specification and inference. We also report exploratory comparisons by competition, financial health, opacity, and period; they do not show a consistent within-firm pattern. DealScan tests using unique facilities likewise show no common relation across facility incidence, spreads, maturity, security, and covenants. The evidence supports an association in the baseline industry-and-year specification, but not a causal claim that firms choose less bank debt to avoid monitoring or that lenders restrict credit because of the index.

items.title: Locally Robust Inference with Outcomes Predicted by Machine Learning
items.summary: Many parameters of interest in economics depend on outcomes generated by machine learning (ML). These generated outcomes are subsequently used in standard econometric estimation and typically treated as observed, a practice that threatens the validity of downstream inference. Relevant examples include the partially linear model with an ML-predicted outcome, productivity persistence, and inequality of opportunity with life-cycle-corrected income. This paper develops a three-step locally robust GMM framework for valid inference when the dependent variable is generated by ML. We construct a debiased moment condition that augments the identifying moment with first- and second-step influence functions, making inference locally insensitive to regularization and model selection biases at both steps. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the locally robust estimator and illustrate its finite-sample performance through simulations. We then estimate inequality of opportunity in Spain, where incomes observed at different ages are subject to life-cycle bias. Correcting income for this bias with type-specific age profiles estimated by ML lowers inequality of opportunity over the working life by 10% to 14% relative to raw income, whereas treating the corrected incomes as observed overstates it by up to 15%.

items.title: Persistence and Change in National Production Networks
items.summary: Many country-years in multi-country input-output databases have no national table. We study the kernel of domestic intermediate transactions, the part that rescaling to new industry totals cannot update. Among 25 economies with a national table every year, the latest table misplaces 6.6 percent of the kernel one year ahead and 21.2 percent ten years ahead, while the five most similar economies misplace 24.1 to 25.0 percent at every horizon. In the OECD tables, 88 percent of country-years without a national table lie close to one cross-country template, against 3.6 percent of country-years with a table. The template spreads from 29 economies in 2019 to 67 in 2022. In this sample an own table's error meets its distance to that year's template near fifteen years, not as a general shelf life.

items.title: The Endogeneity of Miscalibration: Impossibility and Escape in Scored Reporting
items.summary: An agent's probability report is paid for twice: by a strictly proper scoring rule, which rewards accuracy, and by an approval rule for the decision it triggers. An approval rule that is not affine is known to defeat truthful reporting. We show the conflict is built in: whenever perfect screening is attainable, the welfare-maximizing approval rule is never affine. The distortion is predictable: there is a reserve report at which pretending to be the marginal type costs exactly what approval is worth. Approving every report at or above the reserve sorts agents as if their beliefs were observed, under every strictly proper score and for any belief distribution. So does a continuous rule with one corner; under strict feasibility no continuously differentiable rule does. The binding constraint is steepness, not smoothness: a slope-capped rule sorts perfectly if and only if the cap reaches the critical slope, the steepest chord of the pretending cost up to the reserve; below it the welfare loss is cubic in the shortfall. For the Brier, log and power scores, and whenever the pretending cost is convex up to the reserve, the critical slope has a closed form. The instances are AI-agent oversight and marketplace operation.

items.title: The Statistical Cost of Second-Order Orthogonality
items.summary: Debiased machine learning removes the first-order effect of nuisance estimation, but the remaining quadratic bias can invalidate inference when nuisance functions are hard to learn. Second-order orthogonal moments remove this bias at the cost of additional variance. We characterize this cost as the minimum variance of a correction that offsets the quadratic sensitivity of the moment to nuisance errors, and show that exact correction is possible only when this cost is finite. Because the cost varies across moments, the first-order efficient moment need not minimize total variance. We therefore choose the moment and its correction jointly, and derive the resulting minimum variance, a second-order analogue of the semiparametric efficiency bound. The optimal moment may trade first-order efficiency for a lower correction cost. In a binary choice logit model, it uses information beyond the conditional likelihood only in well-populated covariate cells; in difference-in-differences with continuous covariates, exact correction forgoes the efficiency gains from exclusion restrictions. In the partially linear model with continuous controls, the cost is infinite for every moment, so that only part of the bias can be removed. For such cases, we propose a data-driven adaptive rule that chooses how much bias to remove within a bound on variance inflation, and we show that inference remains valid after selection. In simulations for the partially linear model, the coverage of nominal 95\% intervals rises from 32--80\% to 94--97\% in all designs but a stress test.

items.title: Demand reduction and initial endowments in consignment auctions
items.summary: Consignment auctions, in which bidders first receive free initial endowments of a good and must then consign them to a subsequent uniform price auction, are often used in emissions allowance trading for the environmental regulation of greenhouse gas emissions. We study consignment auctions where many asymmetric bidders have flat demands up to their respective quantity constraints. We first characterize the equilibrium outcome and then examine the effects of initial endowments and total supply. If bidders' initial endowments increase or the total supply decreases, the equilibrium price increases whereas the social welfare and the auctioneer's revenue may increase or decrease. In particular, the revenue may increase even though fewer units remain in the hands of the auctioneer since an increase in initial endowments can prevent the low price equilibrium resulting from demand reduction.

items.title: Firm Entry and Exit with Unbounded Productivity
items.summary: In Hopenhayn's (1992) entry-exit model productivity is bounded, implying that the predicted firm size distribution cannot match the power law tail observable in the data. In this paper we remove the boundedness assumption and, in this more general setting, provide an exact characterization of existence of stationary equilibria, as well as a novel sufficient condition for existence based on treating production as a Lyapunov function. We also provide new representations of the rate of entry and aggregate supply. Market clearing rules out stationary competitive equilibria at or below Zipf's law. Under monopolistic competition where the demand for each firm's variety bounds its sales, a stationary equilibrium exists for every tail index of productivity. In an example with additive preferences, unbounded markups inherit the Pareto tail of productivity.

items.title: From Pre-Trends to Bounds: Robust Difference-in-Differences
items.summary: Difference-in-differences is a widely used method for estimating causal effects in non-experimental settings, relying on two key assumptions: the Parallel Trends (PT) assumption and the No-Anticipation Effects (No-AE) assumption. However, the validity of these assumptions are challenging to demonstrate empirically because they rely on unobservable quantities. This paper presents a unified framework that is robust to violations of either or both of these assumptions. By reinterpreting the PT assumption through the lens of selection bias, we introduce the concept of a robust difference-in-differences (RDID) estimand. We derive partial identification results for the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated under relaxed assumptions and characterize a misspecification-robust region based on minimum data-consistent relaxations of the standard model. Furthermore, our framework is extended to accommodate covariates and multiple post-treatment periods.
